articles.title: Election 2026: Republicans, for now, cling to 26-24 majority in state Senate
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Republicans, collectively swept aside by Democrats at every significant turn in the 2026 midterms, may hold a slim 26-24 edge in the No...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Republicans, collectively swept aside by Democrats at every significant turn in the 2026 midterms, may hold a slim 26-24 edge in the North Carolina Senate when final recounts are done.

Already lost Tuesday were the state House of Representatives, a U.S. Senate seat, majority of 14 seats to the U.S. House of Representatives, a state Supreme Court seat and all three seats on the ballot for the North Carolina Court of Appeals.

President Donald Trump for weeks told voters to pretend he was on the ballot; in the Tarheel State, his numbers were far below water and voters didn't seem to have any make believe in solidarity.

With all precincts in, unofficial results have incumbent Republican Sen. Danny Britt ahead of Democrat Catina Hamm by 268 votes in District 24 – a margin within recount request for Hamm. Britt would make it 26-24 Republicans; a Hamm win would tie it at 25 and deliver first-term Democratic Lt. Gov. Rachel Hunt the tie-breaking vote for the chamber.

Democrats won 70 seats in the state House of Representatives and have first-term Gov. Josh Stein. This means the purple state with more than 40% unaffiliated voters is within reach of being a blue trifecta.

Democrats flipped four Republican seats.

In District 4, Jess Rivera defeated Sen. Buck Newton 51.1%-48.9%; in District 7, Jessica Bichler defeated Sen. Michael Lee 52.6%-47.4%; in District 11, James Gailliard defeated Sen. Lisa Barnes 51.4%-46.3%; and in District 34's open seat race, April Cook defeated Kevin Crutchfield 57.7%-42.3%.

District 4 has voters in Greene, Wayne and Wilson counties. Newton, of Wilson, was seeking a sixth term. District 7 has voters only in New Hanover County and Lee was also seeking a sixth term.

District 11 has voters in Franklin, Nash and Vance counties, the largest volume being from Nash. Barnes, of Spring Hope in Nash County, was seeking a fourth term in the Senate following one in the House of Representatives.

District 34 has voters in Cabarrus County. Crutchfield, of Midland, knocked out Republican Sen. Chris Measmer 53.7%-46.3% in the primary. Measmer had been appointed April 8, 2025, filling the term of Republican Sen. Paul Newton after his resignation.

articles.title: Oito anos após criação do 'SUS da Segurança', crime organizado avançou; entenda os desafios da nova política para o setor | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento aponta alta de crimes violentos em cidades menores. Especialistas dizem que colocar sistema na Constituição deve dar mais força à atuação coordenada contra facções.
articles.summary: Levantamento aponta alta de crimes violentos em cidades menores. Especialistas dizem que colocar sistema na Constituição deve dar mais força à atuação coordenada contra facções.
articles.body:
Criado por lei em 2018 para integrar a atuação dos órgãos federais, estaduais e municipais no combate ao crime organizado, o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (Susp) passará a fazer parte da Constituição .

O Senado aprovou nesta terça-feira (3) a chamada PEC da Segurança . Para entrar em vigor, o texto ainda terá de ser promulgado pelo Congresso Nacional.

🔎O sistema será a espinha dorsal da nova política de segurança pública, que dará à União mais poder para coordenar as ações e estabelecer diretrizes nacionais de combate ao crime organizado.

O g1 ouviu especialistas sobre o avanço do crime nesses oito anos desde a criação do SUS da Segurança Pública e sobre os desafios para combatê-lo.

Conselheiro do Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública e pesquisador da Universidade de Coimbra, Roberto Uchôa vê na PEC uma mudança estrutural que a mera criação do Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (Susp), em 2018, não conseguiu representar.

"O Susp foi criado por uma lei ordinária que se tornou praticamente um projeto de intenções, não foi colocado em prática, não se tornou uma política de Estado. Criou-se o Susp mas não se deu, por exemplo, à Polícia Federal a prerrogativa de investigar as organizações criminosas de forma independente, não residual, como agora está sendo feito na PEC. São mudanças estruturais que permitirão que o Susp passe a funcionar", diz Uchôa.

Apesar de estar em lei federal desde 2018, o Susp não conseguiu impedir o avanço de facções no território brasileiro.

Dados do Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública (FBSP) mostram que 41,2% dos brasileiros afirmam haver presença de facções ou milícias no bairro onde moram .

Um dos fatores que demonstram isso é a diversificação da atuação das organizações criminosas no Brasil.

O tráfico de drogas é somente uma das diferentes linhas de atuação de facções no país, mas que também se estende por uma presença internacional.

Outros crimes, como fraudes digitais e estelionato, passaram a fazer parte do dia a dia de facções no país, além de atividades lícitas em que integrantes de facções se infiltram.

O pesquisador afirma que, com a PEC, a PF poderá ter atuação nacional semelhante à que vem tendo no Rio de Janeiro desde a decisão do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) na ADPF das Favelas — que deu à Polícia Federal um papel mais efetivo no combate ao crime organizado no estado.

"Desde então, temos observado a PF fazer várias operações, atacando diversas frentes no Rio de Janeiro: a Unha e Carne, que prendeu o presidente da Assembleia Legislativa. A operação contra a Refit, de sonegação fiscal. Operação contra milícias", diz Uchôa.

"Ou seja, a PF tem atuado em três frentes: na movimentação do dinheiro — contra sonegação fiscal e corrupção de agentes públicos —, na lavagem do dinheiro — quando prendeu o segundo deputado mais votado do Rio, Márcio Canella, que lavava bilhões de reais numa rede de postos —, e no combate à corrupção dentro das instituições públicas — prendeu pessoas na Assembleia, no Tribunal Regional Federal, na polícia", acrescentou o especialista.

Segundo Uchôa, essa atuação é importante "porque não se consegue combater o crime organizado enquanto não combater sua infiltração nas instituições e a lavagem do dinheiro do crime" .

"Mesmo que você faça a retomada pontual de um território dominado, se não tiver feito o combate à corrupção anterior e o combate à lavagem de dinheiro, manter essa organização longe daquele território se torna muito mais difícil", diz Uchôa.

"O papel do governo federal é ajudar nisso. É uma conjugação de forças: a PF não tem efetivo [grande número de homens], mas tem expertise. O estado tem o efetivo, a massa para ocupar o lugar", emenda.

Outro dado que dá a dimensão e complexidade do problema é o da interiorização de organizações criminosas. Uma pesquisa do Instituto de Pesquisa Econômica Aplicada (Ipea) em conjunto com o FBSP mostra que cidades menores do Brasil tiveram alta em crimes violentos, incluindo homicídios.

Há ainda o fato de que o número de facções cresceu expressivamente no país. Diferentemente dos anos 1990, Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) e Comando Vermelho (CV) passaram a ter diferentes organizações com atuações similares. Um exemplo disso é Pernambuco, que tem ao menos 12 facções em conflito, segundo o Ipea.

No Norte brasileiro, por exemplo, foram registradas escaladas em crimes violentos por guerra entre as facções nos últimos anos. Além disso, outras organizações importantes passaram a atuar em estados do Norte, como a Família Terror do Amapá e o Cartel do Norte.

O fenômeno, no entanto, é observado em todo o país, ainda que com conflitos menos públicos, como em Santa Catarina e Minas Gerais.

A advogada e diretora-executiva do Instituto Sou da Paz, Carolina Ricardo, afirma que a coordenação a partir do governo federal pode fortalecer a segurança pública nacional.

Para ela, colocar o Susp na Constituição dá mais força para implementar uma política coordenada, com troca de informações, sistemas e forças-tarefa de combate ao crime organizado no país.

"Essa possibilidade de solicitar e de fazer a gestão de informações compartilhadas no Estado, de ter sistemas interoperáveis, dá um pouco mais de força para o governo federal fazer a coordenação", diz ela.

Apesar disso, a especialista também aponta que, estando ou não na Constituição, o Susp só fará a diferença se essa for uma escolha do presidente ou do ministro responsável pela política de segurança pública .

"O que garante que o Susp saia do papel, seja como uma lei federal, seja na Constituição, é a liderança política do presidente e do ministro, que precisa, eu costumo dizer, acordar e dormir falando em segurança pública", conclui Carolina.

Dados do Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública (FBSP) mostram que 41,2% dos brasileiros afirmam haver presença de facções ou milícias no bairro onde moram — Foto: Joédson Alves/Agência Brasil

articles.title: Bolsonaro pede a Moraes para receber candidatos ao Senado | G1
articles.standfirst: Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) já anunciou que será candidato. Tereza Cristina (PP-MS) indicou que deve participar da disputa, na qual Alcolumbre (União-AP) tentará reeleição.
articles.summary: Bolsonaro pede autorização a Moraes para se reunir com os senadores Rogério Marinho e Tereza Cristina, que articulam candidaturas à presidência do Senado em 2027.
articles.body:
A defesa do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro pediu ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes , do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), autorização para receber visitas dos senadores Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) e Tereza Cristina ( PP -MS) na residência em que cumpre pena por tentativa de golpe.

Ambos os parlamentares foram ministros durante a gestão de Bolsonaro e indicam participação na disputa pela presidência do Senado para o biênio 2027–2028 .

No pedido encaminhado ao ministro do STF, os advogados de Bolsonaro solicitaram que as visitas ocorram em datas a serem fixadas pelo gabinete de Moraes, "preferencialmente às terças, quartas ou quintas-feiras".

A solicitação ocorre em meio às articulações políticas para a eleição da Mesa Diretora do Senado, marcada para a primeira semana de fevereiro . O vencedor precisará reunir a maioria absoluta dos votos da Casa — ao menos 41 dos 81 senadores, em votação secreta.

Nesta semana, a bancada do PL oficializou a pré-candidatura de Rogério Marinho, atual líder da Oposição no Senado. A legenda contará com 29 integrantes a partir de fevereiro de 2027, consolidando-se como a maior bancada da Casa.

O principal adversário de Marinho na disputa é o atual presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre ( União Brasil -AP), que trabalha pela reeleição e reúne apoio de parcelas do centro e de aliados governistas.

Já a senadora Tereza Cristina (PP-MS) também se movimenta para viabilizar sua candidatura no bloco partidário. Ao lançar seu nome, Marinho afirmou que ele e Tereza integram o mesmo campo político e devem atuar de forma coordenada.

Além de comandar o Senado e o Congresso, o presidente da Casa tem entre as atribuições a definição da pauta de votações do plenário e a prerrogativa regimental de dar andamento ou arquivar pedidos de impeachment contra autoridades, incluindo ministros do STF e o procurador-geral da República.

Tereza Cristina e o então presidente Jair Bolsonaro, quando ela era ministra, em 2021 — Foto: Alan Santos/PR

articles.title: ‘Decoy Dan’ could be deciding factor in Alaska Senate race
articles.summary: According to the latest polls, "Decoy Dan" has less than 2% of the vote from Alaskans.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — As the Alaska Senate race votes continue to be tallied, the votes for the wrong Dan Sullivan could be the difference in who wins.

With 74% of the vote counted, the race remains in focus after some voters told NewsNation on Tuesday they were confused by seeing two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

According to the latest polls, "Decoy Dan" has less than 2% of the vote from Alaskans.

NewsNation tracked down a "paranoid" Alaska voter over the weekend, who said, "I might be just having a brain freeze, but I don't remember the second Dan Sullivan. I definitely intended to vote for the real Dan Sullivan."

Wrong Dan Sullivan's votes could decide Alaska winner

Despite the razor-thin margins, former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola remains upbeat about her chances of securing victory after the Democrats' landslide victory. DDHQ polls noted Peltola leads Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan by less than one percentage point.

Peltola paid no mind to the ballot scandal allegations in a New York Times report that said Peltola's campaign worked with people trying to recruit Dan J. Sullivan to run for Senate in a "ballot composition project."

Sullivan balked at Peltola's remarks, stating, "My opponent has run her campaign on literally from the beginning, purposely misleading Alaskans, cheating, and then lying for the last year and a half."

The deadline for absentee ballots in the state isn't till Nov. 18.

NewsNation's Dylan Furbay contributed to this report.

articles.title: Rep. Ro Khanna allies launch a draft campaign for the 2028 presidential race
articles.summary: Exclusive: The California congressman has been traveling the country and building prominence among progressives.
articles.body: Allies of Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., are launching an effort to lay groundwork for him to run for president, the leaders of a new draft committee told NBC News. Former Rep. Jamaal Bowman, D-N.Y., and progressive strategist Nomiki Konst are co-chairs of the group — “Run Ro” — which can raise money from donors and begin building support for a Khanna candidacy while he continues to weigh a 2028 bid. The move comes in the immediate aftermath of a midterm election in which voters swept Democrats into power in the House and the Senate, with some high-profile progressives among the big winners. It also comes as the party’s left wing looks for a new champion who can run in the progressive lane that Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., occupied in the 2016 and 2020 presidential nominating contests. “By launching now, we are trying to ensure that the presidential primary debate is framed from a progressive populist perspective,” Konst said. The challenges facing a possible Khanna candidacy are immense. Only one person was ever elected to the presidency directly from the House: James Garfield, R-Ohio, in 1880. Khanna, a fifth-term lawmaker, has made headlines with bipartisan efforts to force the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files and to end the war in Iran. He is nonetheless not even the most famous House progressive considering a presidential bid. That unofficial title belongs to Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., who hasn’t yet said whether she will seek the presidency, run for a Senate seat in New York or remain in the House. “She is my sister, and I love her,” Bowman said of Ocasio-Cortez, with whom he shared a close alliance in the House. “Ro Khanna has shown the work ethic, the humility and the vision that we need in this moment.” Khanna, who was a co-chair of Sanders’ 2020 campaign, is also a favorite of progressives around the country. And he has been traveling to early primary states for months. He makes no effort to hide his presidential ambitions, and many of his colleagues believe he will jump into the race. He welcomed the draft committee in a statement to NBC News. “I’m honored that people are encouraging me to run on a platform of Medicare for All, ending foreign wars and taxing the billionaires,” he said. “We need America’s Next New Deal. Whether I run or support someone else is something I will decide with my family after the holidays.” Konst said the draft committee will allow her and Bowman to organize now so Khanna isn’t late to the game if he does run. “The centrists organize and strategize early,” she said. “They have their donors, corporate consultants and leaders lined up for years. Building off the lessons of past primaries, our goal is to channel the progressive energy into a vessel for organizing and spreading our winning message early, as we can’t wait for the politics to line up.” No candidate has yet entered the field for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

articles.title: LEE CARTER: The biggest winner of this election is not who you think
articles.summary: This election proved persuasion still works in American democracy, showing that voters aren't permanently locked into political teams or tribal loyalties.
articles.body: Whether you’re celebrating this week's midterm elections or sniffling into your morning coffee, I have some good news. And no, it has nothing to do with which party won. For years, we’ve been told that America is hopelessly divided. That our politics are tribal. That our opinions are fixed, our loyalties inherited, and our minds about as open as a bank on Christmas. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI Democrats vote for Democrats. Republicans vote for Republicans. Independents insist they’re independent while somehow managing to vote for the same party every November. Persuasion? Forget it. Why bother making an argument when everyone has already made up their mind? LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN Well, guess what? They haven’t. And that may be the most encouraging thing to come out of this election. I’m a researcher and strategist. I spend my life studying what people believe, why they believe it, and what, if anything, might change their minds. I even wrote a book called" Persuasion," which lately has been beginning to sound like a work of historical fiction. JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026 But I’ll admit something. Watching our politics harden over the past decade, even I began to wonder just how persuadable America really was. We seemed to have reached a point where facts were filtered through party affiliation, arguments were judged by who made them, and changing your mind was treated less like intellectual growth and more like treason. In the 2026 midterm elections, voters just did something wonderfully inconvenient. They reminded us that they are human beings, not permanent members of political teams. We’ve stopped debating and started diagnosing. Anyone who disagrees with us must be stupid, evil, brainwashed or watching the wrong cable news channel. Then voters did something wonderfully inconvenient. They reminded us that they are human beings, not permanent members of political teams. Look at Michigan. Look at Texas. Look at Kansas. EVERYONE IS WATCHING TEXAS AND MICHIGAN. AS A POLLSTER, I KNOW WHERE THE REAL STORY IS Different states. Different political traditions. Different electorates. But each offers a reason to question the assumption that political identity is destiny. Candidates can still reach people who weren’t necessarily inclined to listen. An argument can still break through. A message that speaks to something voters genuinely care about can still make them reconsider what they thought they knew. Of course, an election result alone doesn’t tell us precisely how many voters changed their minds and how many different voters simply showed up. As a researcher, I feel compelled to point that out, even at the risk of ruining a perfectly good argument. But the larger lesson remains. INDEPENDENT VOTERS AREN’T PICKING A POLITICAL TEAM, THEY JUST FEEL PICKED ON Political coalitions are not permanent. And voters are not property. That’s not a flaw in democracy. That’s democracy working. We’ve spent so much time talking about polarization that we’ve started treating it as a permanent condition. As though Americans arrived at the voting booth with their opinions tattooed on their foreheads. But Americans are more complicated than their party registrations. They can be conservative about spending and liberal about healthcare. Frustrated with immigration and worried about government overreach. Loyal to a president and disappointed in his party. Angry at Washington and hopeful about their hometown. They can hold two seemingly contradictory ideas at once. Imagine that. THE HISPANIC VOTE IS UP FOR GRABS IN 2026. CANDIDATES WHO IGNORE IT WILL LOSE And most importantly, they can change their minds. Not necessarily because someone shouted louder. Not because a campaign spent another $50 million telling them the other guy was terrible. And certainly not because a celebrity told them what to think. But because someone made an argument that connected with their lives. That is what persuasion actually is. Whether your candidates won or lost, whether you’re popping champagne or reaching for the tissues, take a little comfort in this: America isn’t as stuck as we thought. It’s not tricking people. It’s not manipulating them. It’s not finding the magic words that make people abandon their values. It’s finding the truth in your argument that connects with the truth in someone else’s life. And when that happens, something remarkable becomes possible. I'M JESSICA TARLOV, AND SOMETIMES I GET IT WRONG. ACCEPTING THAT IS THE FIRST STEP TOWARDS BETTER DEBATES A voter can cross a party line. A lifelong loyalist can reconsider. Someone who has tuned out politics altogether can decide that this time, something is worth paying attention to. None of this means America is suddenly united. Far from it. We still disagree, often fiercely. We still retreat into our corners. We still have a remarkable talent for assuming the worst about people who vote differently from us. And Thanksgiving dinner is still going to require a seating chart and possibly a referee. But disagreement is not the same thing as permanence. And division is not the same thing as hopelessness. The Founders didn’t build a country on the assumption that everyone would agree. They built one in which disagreement could be argued, debated, challenged and ultimately resolved, at least temporarily, by the people. A country of ideas and ideals. A country where arguments are supposed to matter. Where leaders have to earn support rather than simply inherit it. Where no party owns a voter forever. And where the best ideas have a chance to win, provided someone can make the case for them. That’s the part I hope we don’t miss in all the post-election analysis. Because if minds can change, then our future isn’t predetermined by our divisions. If voters can be persuaded, politicians have a reason to listen. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION If people are willing to reconsider what they believe, the rest of us have a reason to keep talking to one another. And if an election can surprise us, perhaps our neighbors can, too. So, whether your candidates won or lost, whether you’re popping champagne or reaching for the tissues, take a little comfort in this: America isn’t as stuck as we thought. People are still listening. Arguments still matter. Ideas can still change minds. And in a country that has spent years being told it’s hopelessly divided, that might be the most hopeful election result of all. articles.title: MEHEK COOKE: Republicans failed the affordability test. This is how to win voters back
articles.summary: Republicans lost Tuesday's elections because voters graded the GOP on groceries, gasoline, housing and healthcare affordability, not ideology.
articles.body: Republicans lost Tuesday because we forgot the oldest lesson in politics: It is the economy, stupid. Americans did not suddenly embrace socialism or bigger government. Instead, they graded the GOP on a pocketbook scorecard of groceries, gasoline, housing and healthcare, then punished Republicans for failing to deliver financial relief they could feel. Democrats captured both chambers of Congress, flipped governor’s offices and won statewide races across the country, including in Ohio, which President Donald Trump carried by double digits two years ago. Republicans must recognize that this election was a performance review and not simply the product of media bias, poor turnout or an ideological transformation of the country. The warning was clear before a single vote was counted. A Fox News poll found that 60% of voters considered the cost of living their greatest economic concern, 74% rated the economy negatively and only 18% said their families were better off than two years earlier. Election Day was not a repudiation of every Republican principle. Voters still trusted the GOP more on crime, border security and immigration, but those advantages did not close the affordability gap. TRUMP PLEDGES TO VETO 'INSANE' DEM BILLS, PINPOINTS ISSUE PARTIALLY TO BLAME FOR REPUBLICAN LOSSES Republicans won the White House and both chambers in 2024 by promising economic relief, and voters judged the delivery of that promise through their bank accounts. Abandoning conservative principles would deliver more victories to Democrats and dismissing the losses as nothing more than anti-Trump anger would ignore the financial plea voters made. President Trump delivered tax relief, but Republicans failed to make broader affordability gains arrive quickly enough for families to feel them. Democrats respond to government failure by demanding more government. They point to unaffordable housing and medical bills, invoke affordability and then call for larger budgets, new programs and expanded federal authority. Republicans cannot respond with abstract defenses of limited government while existing institutions remain expensive and unreliable. The next Republican revolution must be a competence revolution focused on lowering the cost of living and putting American interests first. That requires government to perform its essential duties, enforce the law and remove barriers preventing families and businesses from succeeding. While Democrats measure government by how much it spends, Republicans must measure it by what families save. The clearest opportunity to close the delivery gap is healthcare. A post-election KFF analysis of the national voter poll found that voters trusted Democrats over Republicans by 19 points on the issue. More than half said Trump administration policies had made their own healthcare costs worse, while only 10% said those costs had improved. Healthcare is a major pocketbook issue, and voters judged Republicans by how much they are paying for their medical bills. More promises won’t change that sentiment, but a plan that enforces price transparency, exposes hidden middleman markups, increases competition and requires timely explanations of coverage denials would. That is competent government because it gives patients information and choices without creating a larger federal healthcare system. Democratic control of both chambers of Congress still leaves President Trump with the power of the veto pen even as he pledges to work with Democrats. This gives him significant negotiating leverage because Democrats need his signature to enact legislation unless they secure two-thirds support in both chambers. President Trump’s power to say no allows him to reject legislation that makes life more expensive while demanding affordability provisions that provide measurable relief for families. Democrats are now on notice. They must show voters whether they really stand for affordability or just a larger spending agenda. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Congressional Republicans face the same affordability mandate. Every spending bill, regulatory proposal and policy should be measured by whether it lowers healthcare costs, removes barriers to building housing, reduces government waste and allows families to keep more of what they earn. The Trump administration and Republican governors should publish scorecards that measure permit processing times, taxpayer dollars protected from fraud and whether government programs deliver what they promised. Before spending more money on a failing program, Republicans should also require an audit explaining what went wrong, where the existing money went and what taxpayers would receive from any additional spending. The test is not whether a proposal is red or blue, but whether it leaves more green in Americans’ wallets. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Democrats failed to offer a coherent governing strategy beyond blaming President Trump, and they are already mistaking Tuesday’s victory for an endorsement of socialism, permission to expand government and a blank check to spend two years investigating the president. That mistake gives Republicans a clear opportunity to prove that conservative principles can make life more affordable. Tuesday was a warning that principles without competent delivery will not earn another majority. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM MEHEK COOKE

articles.title: Republicans sort through election carnage for a message ahead of a new era
articles.summary: Republicans woke up Wednesday morning licking their wounds after a shellacking in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Many are now determining what the path forward for their party ought to be and how far to push back on President Trump from the minority. After enjoying a governing trifecta for the first two years of the second Trump…
articles.body:
Republicans woke up Wednesday morning licking their wounds after a shellacking in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Many are now determining what the path forward for their party ought to be and how far to push back on President Trump from the minority.

After enjoying a governing trifecta for the first two years of the second Trump presidency, where extreme deference to the president was the law of the land, Republicans are staring down a new political reality.

They aren’t even sure whether to blame their own leaders.

While the top Republicans in the Senate are likely to stay the same, a leadership shake-up is on deck in the House as Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) will not seek to be minority leader.

In their initial responses to the massive electoral losses, Republicans acknowledged the effect of the war in Iran and high prices, especially for gasoline, on voters’ attitudes.

Vice President Vance, a likely contender to succeed Trump in 2028, explicitly blamed Republicans’ losses on the war in Iran.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a lengthy post Wednesday on social platform X. “The president himself said so last night.”

Vance’s critique was an extraordinary acknowledgment that his administration’s handling of the war has become a political liability for Republicans, even as Trump continues to defend it.

Other Republicans, while stopping short of criticizing Trump directly, indicated that the time was ripe for more resistance from Congress to his agenda.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), in an interview with a South Dakota reporter , suggested Republicans may conduct their own long-delayed oversight of the administration.

“We’ll do our best to respect the office of the presidency, to work with the president, to try to move forward in terms of building our economy,” Rounds said. “But we’re also going to have to take a second look at some of the executive branch decisions that have been made, and we’ll try to add our two cents in and maybe make them a little bit better.”

Douglas Heye, a longtime Republican strategist, told The Hill he felt the election loss was “inevitable.”

“As Trump denied the reality of what voters felt and his approval rating became a never-ending limbo contest of how low can it go, hoarding money and veering bizarrely off message, this self-created Trump Quake was inevitable,” Heye said. “Where the party goes from here — no one knows.”

On Wednesday, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) said he thinks there’s Republican support for ending the Iran war as soon as possible. Schumer said Democrats would likely use the “power of the purse” to starve the Defense Department of funding if necessary.

There are also already Republicans more openly calling for a rethinking of the party platform, which has become synonymous with Trump’s wishes.

Chief among those critics is Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost his primary to Trump-backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who subsequently lost to Democrat James Talarico on Tuesday.

Cornyn, in an op-ed Wednesday for The Wall Street Journal, accused Trump of “misreading the mandate” that voters gave him and the party in 2024 and cited tariffs, “hyperaggressive immigration enforcement,” the Iran war and Trump signaling “disconnection by focusing on sideshows like swimming-pool liners in the Reflecting Pool.”

Cornyn also criticized his party for promoting unlikeable candidates like Paxton and Rep. Mike Collins — who lost the Senate race in Georgia — with too many scandals and character flaws.

Republicans lost because they had forgotten how to build a political coalition and instead “shrank the tent,” Cornyn wrote.

“In Texas, statewide candidate Bo French poisoned the well even further with blatant bigotry against Indian-Americans, anathema to the party of Lincoln and Reagan. When nominees show contempt for voters and request a smaller Republican Party, voters oblige them,” Cornyn wrote.

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) implicated similar problems in an essay on Substack Tuesday night and called for a philosophical solution: restoring traditional values of the conservative movement espoused by former President Reagan and the pioneers.

“We know from experience, not just theory, that a truly conservative policy agenda fosters the greatest chance for human flourishing—marked by robust economic opportunity, stronger families and households, and a global order led by the United States with help from its democratic allies and partners,” Curtis wrote.

Sen. John Barrasso (Wyo.), Republican whip, said in a post on X that “there are clear lessons” from the election results and that he’s “here for the fight,” but he did not provide much detail.

“Senate Republicans have an opportunity and obligation to show our voters that we are fighting for them,” Barrasso wrote. “In the Senate, we will aggressively oppose terrible ideas that drive our country toward the socialism Democrats embraced. Our commitment is to common sense.” He continued that Republicans’ focus should not waver “from the top priority of driving down prices that have remained stubbornly high.”

Outside groups that have been influential in the GOP so far are also weighing in, with some equally scorching Trump and others suggesting guideposts for the party’s next moves.

Chip Wyatt, government relations director for the Senate at Heritage Action, told The Hill he sees opportunity in the Republican policies that voters aligned with on ballot measures.

In California, for example, voters are looking likely to reject a wealth tax.

In Colorado, voters are on track to approve a ballot measure banning gender confirmation surgeries for minors and one requiring student athletes to participate in sports teams according to their sex assigned at birth.

Similar measures related to student-athletes passed Arizona and Nebraska, and one was looking likely to pass in Washington state as of Wednesday afternoon.

Other states approved ballot measures requiring voter ID verification or proof of citizenship to vote, in line with Republicans’ highly sought Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act that Congress hasn’t taken up.

Those issues, Wyatt said, could be “wedges” that Republicans could continue to lean into for popular support against Democrats.

“When we look at the states, we’re able to look at the individual ballot measures that people are voting for, again, like ostensibly Republican policies that are doing well,” Wyatt said. “I think that provides a good road map for things that the party ought to look to for the future.”

articles.title: Mississippi has an unexpectedly close Senate race but no recount procedure
articles.summary: The Mississippi Senate race could be headed for the courts, as two candidates are locked in a tight contest with no recount procedure on the books. The election between Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom remained too close to call as of Wednesday evening, with Colom leading by less than a quarter of…
articles.body:
The Mississippi Senate race could be headed for the courts, as two candidates are locked in a tight contest with no recount procedure on the books.

The election between Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom remained too close to call as of Wednesday evening, with Colom leading by less than a quarter of a percentage point. That’s fewer than 2,000 votes.

And ballots are still coming in. The state allows mail ballots to be counted so long as they were postmarked by Election Day and received up to five business days later, a law that was upheld by the Supreme Court this summer. Mississippi is still waiting to see if roughly 3,600 outstanding ballots show up in time, according to the state’s top election official.

In addition to those, Colom’s campaign put the count for provisional ballots at around 15,000 on Election Day — but both sides are holding their breath.

“We are going to make sure every single vote has been counted, and I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat,” Colom said in a post on the social platform X on election night.

Hyde-Smith assured supporters at a campaign watch party she wasn’t going anywhere.

“I’ll tell you the Democrats got out and worked, they really got out and worked, and a lot of them showed up today. But not enough of them. I’ll just tell you that right now,” the senator said, according to Mississippi Today . “I assure you I will continue to be your U.S. senator.”

The final margins may well determine what happens next. A wide swing in either direction could soften the chance of legal challenges, but a close result could have the loser’s lawyers racing to court.

“In some states, you know, a really close election automatically triggers a recount. That’s not true in Mississippi,” said Ronald Rychlak, a professor at the University of Mississippi Law School. “In fact, a candidate does not have an automatic right to a recount, even if they offer to pay for it in Mississippi.”

State law establishes specific procedures for Mississippi Legislature candidates to contest the election. And if it were a county-level race, for example, state law would give candidates a 20-day window. “The candidate or the party has to go in front of the court and make the case,” Rychlak said. “So instead of it being sort of an automatic thing, there is an evidentiary basis that has to be established, and there are procedures in place to help the party gather evidence to make that evidentiary basis.”

But when it comes to federal offices like the U.S. Senate, nothing in Mississippi law provides an express way to contest the general election. It effectively leaves it up to judges to determine how disputes are resolved in any push by either side.

“You might not recount every precinct, and maybe a recount is sought in a particular area because that’s where the evidence suggests that there may have been mistakes made,” Rychlak said. “Then there would be a determination as to whether there was sufficient evidence set forth, and a court at that point could order, you know, a full or partial recount of the votes.”

The lack of clarity is an anomaly. Other states have rules for handling challenges to congressional results, but Mississippi’s are limited to primaries only.

Chris McDaniel attempted to contest the results of the GOP Senate primary after losing to Thad Cochran in 2014, alleging voter fraud. The state Republican executive committee declined to review the complaint because McDaniel had missed the 20-day cutoff. The Mississippi Supreme Court later agreed .

As Mississippi begins to sort out this year’s unexpectedly close race, there’s also the question of how Congress itself will react. The Constitution gives each chamber the power to “be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members.”

There’s another reason the answer may still take time. National Republicans took a Supreme Court loss earlier this year on when mail ballots can be counted, and now the party is grappling with the real-world implications.

In June, the high court ruled 5-4 that federal law does not preempt Mississippi and more than a dozen other states from accepting mail ballots that arrive after Election Day, so long as they were postmarked by then.

Responding to the ruling against the Republican National Committee (RNC), the committee’s chair, Joe Gruters, said: “Republicans are not going to be deterred by this decision, and the RNC will keep fighting to have elections end on Election Day as Americans want.”

But now, the party may need to rely on those votes to swing back into the lead in Mississippi. Decision Desk HQ estimated that roughly 8,500 ballots were still outstanding as of Wednesday, and many of the remaining ballots will be those last-arriving mail ballots.

Republicans for years attempted to shoot down the practice, which became more widespread in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Adding to the sting was that the Supreme Court’s rejection was authored by Justice Amy Coney Barrett, one of President Trump’s own appointees. She took on relentless public attacks from conservatives for it.

Although the justice perhaps wasn’t envisioning a nail-biter Senate race this year, Barrett conceded at the time it was a “significant concern” that Mississippi’s results could give rise to the appearance of fraud if the results “appear to flip after Election Day.”

Still, Barrett said that isn’t the Supreme Court’s problem.

“Election fraud and its appearance are serious issues. Like other such issues, however, they must be addressed through the democratic process,” she wrote.

It means that Mississippi is continuing to accept mail ballots through Nov. 10, five business days after polls closed.

“With the vote as close as it [is], that means we’re going to have to wait to make sure that those are all in,” Rychlak said. “We really have to count every ballot this time, and that means we have to until we have every ballot.”

articles.title: Democrats signal oversight blitz as Trump officials lawyer up
articles.summary: Democrats made clear after Tuesday’s stunning midterm victories that they will use their historic gains in Congress to flex their investigative muscles, swiftly issuing warnings to Trump administration officials they say have thus far dodged their oversight. “Lawyer up,” was the two-word statement issued by incoming House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair Robert Garcia…
articles.body:
Democrats made clear after Tuesday’s stunning midterm victories that they will use their historic gains in Congress to flex their investigative muscles, swiftly issuing warnings to Trump administration officials they say have thus far dodged their oversight.

“Lawyer up,” was the two-word statement issued by incoming House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), whose side of the panel has already lobbed a number of inquiries at Trump administration officials.

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) was even more brief, posting online only “Subpoenas” — a reminder that the party will now have the power to compel testimony from the administration and beyond.

“We’re going to bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption on this country,” Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), set to be the next House Speaker, told those gathered at a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee watch party Tuesday night.

“Because if you have people in high office who are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends or their donors, then they’re not focused on making life better for the American people. But House Democrats will put the American people first.”

Some Democrats were quick to outline priorities for the year ahead.

Garcia’s team indicated it would be investigating “The Trump Crime Family, Crony corporations ripping off the American people, Corrupt Trump admin officials profiting off the presidency, Associates of Jeffrey Epstein” and then specifically called out Corey Lewandowski, who stands accused of funneling contracts at the Department of Homeland Security to allies.

Meanwhile, House Judiciary Committee Democrats on Wednesday issued a job posting for new oversight, investigative and legislative counsel.

“House Judiciary Democrats are prepared to put an end to the rampant and out-of-control corruption overflowing the Trump swamp,” the committee wrote Wednesday on social platform X.

“Through investigations and legislation we will work to expose, counter and dismantle the grift and the graft, the ongoing corruption of government and the outrageous destruction of the rule of law. We will be unflinching in our defense of the Constitution and the Bill of Rights.”

And House Homeland Security Committee Democrats told Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to “clear your calendar.”

The remarks show Democrats’ eagerness to ignite probes and return to those already underway — as well as the overlapping territories that could lead to turf wars in the party.

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), now set to become the House Judiciary chair, has an interest in President Trump reaping financial benefits from the presidency, with the former constitutional law professor staking out a longtime interest in gifts and other payments to the president he says violate the Emoluments Clause of the Constitution.

But Garcia has also flagged his interest in those “profiting off the presidency.”

He’s already sent letters to Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Kimberly Guilfoyle, who was seen in text messages asking for money from a Trump ally to pay off her credit card debt ahead of her confirmation hearing to become ambassador to Greece. Garcia is also interested in another letter about a Russian oligarch’s contributions to Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding.

Several committees have also already undertaken investigations into Trump’s immigration enforcement — a topic shared by three committees in the House and two in the Senate.

Jeffries’s office did not respond to a request for comment on how leadership would navigate dueling interests from various panels.

But some lines are already clearly drawn. Garcia will continue to run point on the investigation into deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, while Raskin is investigating donations Trump received by those he later pardoned, the pressure campaign the White House put on law firms that later agreed to do pro bono work into preferred topics and the ongoing investigation into the Justice Department’s anti-weaponization fund.

Democrats have not been gun-shy about launching probes but admit that many of their requests have simply been met with silence by the Trump administration.

That challenge has not evaporated just because Democrats have returned to power.

The Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) penned a memo earlier this year arguing that executive privilege covers the president’s conversations with outside advisers — something many saw as an attempt by the Trump administration to rebuff future Democratic inquiries.

The argument is likely to be challenged in court once it is asserted, but that court battle could be lengthy, and one senior Democratic staffer said it could play a role in how the party reinitiates some of its investigations.

“In an investigative posture, it’s easier for us to get friendly information with less hostile actors now, and then we can go after the big fish, right?” the staffer said.

“We definitely fight that [OLC opinion] in court, but it doesn’t mean we can’t start doing our due diligence and reupping those requests … going back to big law firms and say, ‘This is your last shot to cooperate, volunteer.’”

There are signs administration officials were a step ahead of Garcia.

The Wall Street Journal reported last month that Cabinet secretaries down to mid-level staffers have already retained counsel . Officials are preparing for probes into Trump’s efforts to build a new ballroom, golf course, and memorial to himself, as well as his dealings with the Kennedy Center. Firms are unlikely to be able to represent numerous staffers who may be implicated in the same probe, leaving administration officials scrambling to secure their preferred firms.

However, administration officials are also already chiming in to indicate they plan to try to stall Democratic oversight.

After Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), a member of the House Homeland Committee, told a series of high-level Trump immigration officials — Mullin as well as border czar Tom Homan and White House aide Stephen Miller — to make themselves available, the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) top lawyer pushed back.

“It is unfortunate that Democrats are more interested in political shenanigans than in governing,” James Percival, DHS’s general counsel, wrote on X.

“Rest assured, however, that we are well prepared to deal with this nonsense so Secretary Mullin can continue focusing on protecting the homeland.”

articles.title: Iran strikes kept quiet during midterm homestretch set off worries about transparency
articles.summary: A series of reported secret U.S. military attacks carried out against Iran in the lead-up to Tuesday’s midterm elections is raising alarms around public tran...
articles.body:
A series of reported secret U.S. military attacks carried out against Iran in the lead-up to Tuesday's midterm elections is raising alarms around public transparency.

The United States's Monday strike on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz — including an antiaircraft facility on the strategic Qeshm Island — marked the latest in a series of American attacks over the past few weeks, The Wall Street Journal first reported. The military operations have not been publicly acknowledged by the U.S. or Iran, and the Pentagon has not disclosed any bombing of Iranian targets since two days of strikes in early September.

President Trump on Tuesday insisted there was no return to fighting, calling the Monday attack "minor" rather than a return to all-out war, a message at odds with his insistence last month that Washington would "not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections."

That, coupled with the Pentagon's silence around a deeply unpopular war as Americans were set to head to the polls, calls into question exactly how much the government is obligated to disclose to the public about its military operations.

Rachel VanLandingham, a former Air Force judge advocate and now a law professor at Southwestern Law School, said there is no clear statutory requirement for the executive branch to publicly disclose discrete military operations.

During previous wars like those in Iraq and Afghanistan, the Pentagon held regular press briefings to keep the public informed, "a norm that has been greatly deviated from under [Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's] Pentagon, which has taken concrete steps to squash transparency," she told The Hill.

One former Pentagon spokesperson had a far more blunt assessment, telling The Hill that the administration "bombed Qeshm Island during a news cycle where no one is going to cover this." He pointed to the timing as falling less than a day before the midterms.

"To the extent that this is incredibly unpopular, they probably don't want a lot of people talking about it," the former spokesperson said. "The lack of disclosure raises real transparency concerns."

U.S. Central Command, the military arm that oversees warfighters in the Middle East, did not respond to questions from The Hill on any recent U.S. strikes on Iran.

It's unsurprising the Trump administration would look to tamp down potential coverage around the Iran war, a conflict that has stretched more than eight months, roiled global markets and sent fuel costs soaring with no relief in sight, with fuel prices proving a major consideration as Americans headed to the voting booth Tuesday.

Washington and Tehran have continued to exchange strikes since this summer but have not returned to the intense missile and drone barrages seen in the early stages of the conflict.

"I think it's clear that the White House was trying to keep the conflict part of this Iran war quieter and not allow it at the near zero hour to hurt its electoral chances or become a factor in the domestic election more than it already was," said Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute.

On Monday, Trump insisted the conflict in Iran is not a forever war, but a "soft war" that he could end at any time he chooses.

"We're not fighting a war. ... When was the last time we fired anything? This isn't a war, this is a very soft war," Trump told Fox News's Sean Hannity shortly after the U.S. military struck Qeshm Island. "This is not much of a war, Sean, because there hasn't been shooting for months."

But following an astonishing GOP loss in the midterms, with Democrats taking back both the House and the Senate by unforeseen numbers, Vice President Vance on Wednesday broke his silence , saying: "The reason we lost is the war."

Trump, meanwhile, told reporters Wednesday that he knew the war would impact voting, but "whether it impacted it or not, Iran can't have a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."

Public information on the war has dropped to all but a trickle, with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth declining to hold any press briefings on the matter since this spring. The Pentagon chief has been particularly hostile to reporters from legacy outlets — banishing them from the Pentagon's hallways without an escort back in October 2025 — and any negative coverage surrounding the conflict.

The former Pentagon spokesperson said in a typical administration, for every kinetic strike the agency would release a statement shortly after the fact, and the current secretary of Defense generally would offer remarks about it, but there are no laws stipulating that must be the case.

"It's not illegal to not do it," the former spokesperson said of public disclosure. "Nixon bombed Cambodia and didn't tell anybody about it for two days. It wasn't a crime. But it's just a thing that's done."

But they added that there are "no more norms of media engagement from the Pentagon. All that has gone away."

As to what an administration is legally required to disclose, VanLandingham said there are overlapping requirements to inform certain members of Congress of certain operations, but not for general public disclosure.

The War Powers Resolution requires the president to provide periodic updates on the status, scope and duration of a war or deployment to Congress every six months, "but that's about the only real statutory reporting requirement — after the initial report within 48 hours of initiation of hostilities or deployment into an area in which hostilities are imminent — for the war in general," she said.

There are also several congressionally mandated provisions in the annual National Defense Authorization Act that require disclosure of U.S. military fatalities to family members.

"Accountability is impossible without transparency, and that's the administration's goal here — to avoid accountability for their wartime actions," VanLandingham added.

articles.title: Midterm shellacking shakes up GOP 2028 presidential landscape
articles.summary: The massive Democratic victories across the country on Tuesday are shaking up the 2028 presidential landscape for Republicans and raising questions about how badly Vice President Vance will be damaged in the fallout. Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, including in red strongholds like Texas and South Carolina, in what was seen as…
articles.body:
The massive Democratic victories across the country on Tuesday are shaking up the 2028 presidential landscape for Republicans and raising questions about how badly Vice President Vance will be damaged in the fallout.

Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, including in red strongholds like Texas and South Carolina, in what was seen as the strongest rebuke of President Trump yet.

The losses have left Republican presidential contenders including Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the awkward position of central figures in a clearly unpopular administration.

“If you want to be the Republican president in 2028, not just the nominee, but actually the person who sits behind the Resolute Desk, you have to be close enough to Trump to win the primary, but not so close that he drags you down in the general,” said Trump’s former chief of staff Mick Mulvaney.

“That is a tall order,” Mulvaney added. “Of course, Trump’s ability to rehabilitate himself is almost superhuman, so that calculus could easily change in the next 12 to 18 months. But if he doesn’t, it will be difficult sledding.”

Many Republicans point to Vance as the biggest loser of the potential 2028 contenders, considering he spent political capital in many key races that were lost and is Trump’s second-in-command.

Tim Chapman, president of Advancing American Freedom, said these results “100 percent” will transform the 2028 presidential landscape.

“You cannot experience a once-in-100-year tsunami-like election and conclude that the status quo is acceptable,” Chapman said. “You just can’t do that, and you certainly cannot experience repudiation like that and conclude that there should be a coronation going into 2028.”

“Compared to 24 hours ago, this is a completely different world,” he added. “And what the world looks like now is that the American people have told Republicans you need to rethink your approach to politics.”

Vance’s supporters are taking a rosier approach, noting that his role in the administration gives him the best launchpad to the presidency.

“Everybody in the administration is going to be tied politically to the challenges that we saw last night. Everybody is kind of hurt equally,” said Chris Johnson, an Ohio Republican strategist.

“He’s the vice president. He’s the next guy, and I think folks are going to be looking for somebody who is going to say hard truths about what happened yesterday and also have a vision for the future that’s going to work in the next election,” he continued.

One GOP strategist said the election results may have done slight damage to Vance’s odds, but not much.

“Did it diminish them? Yes, but he is still the favorite,” the strategist said.

The vice president, who has not announced a 2028 bid, blamed his party’s widespread losses on the Iran war, which he was an opponent of within the administration.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post on the social platform X, urging Republicans to use their anger to “get back to the work of saving our country.”

Additionally, the vice president listed four answers from former GOP voters to a pollster on what it would take for them to come back to the party fold: ending the war, focusing on the cost of living and inflation, putting America first, and changing the U.S. relationship with Israel.

“Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats,” the vice president wrote.

Trump responded to Vance’s statement on Wednesday, telling reporters that he “thought it was good.”

However, Trump did not say whether Vance or anyone else was launching a 2028 bid.

“We will see what happens,” he told reporters. “You don’t know who’s talking about running.”

“Maybe you have a lot of people running. Maybe nobody’s going to run. Maybe he won’t run. I don’t know who’s going to run,” he said.

No major Republicans have formally announced presidential ambitions, but early jockeying for 2028 appeared to have kicked off among some lawmakers hours after the initial results came in.

Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.), who was reelected on Tuesday, told Fox News Digital that he was throwing his support behind Rubio following the GOP’s midterm performance.

“I think the challenge for Marco is the challenge for anybody who wants to be the 2028 nominee — you’ve got to find a way to fuse together a coalition that right now is at war with itself,” Chapman said.

Meanwhile, speculation has been swirling around Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R ), who locked horns with Trump in the 2024 Republican primary. DeSantis was arguably one of the few GOP winners of election night, keeping his state red amidst a blue tsunami, albeit by a narrow margin.

DeSantis, who is term-limited and leaving office in January, wasted no time touting Republican victories in Florida and offering his own assessment of what went wrong for the party nationally.

“To call it a wave would, I don’t think would be fully accurate. It’s the political equivalent of a meteor strike,” the governor said in a press conference on Wednesday morning.

“The one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of Florida,” he said.

Some Republicans think a governor leading their party in 2028 is the way to go.

“DeSantis, Kemp, and even Youngkin are the smart play for our party,” said a second Republican strategist, referring to Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin. The strategist added that they believe DeSantis is open to the prospect.

However, there are questions about whether DeSantis would be able to fit into the Republican Party dominated by Trump’s MAGA movement after losing to the president in 2024.

“I don’t think that matters because MAGA won’t be the same MAGA without Trump,” the strategist said, adding, “JD won’t have access to the same MAGA either.”

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) has also found himself near the top of lists of potential Republican 2028 contenders and has not ruled out having presidential ambitions.

Vance even said in an interview with NBC News last month that it was “really obvious” Cruz was running for president, prompting Cruz to suggest Vance was “feeling insecure.”

However, the massive Republican losses in Texas could spell trouble for Cruz.

“As the sole statewide [Republican] in Texas, he can’t leave and run for president while also helping lead a GOP state recovery. He has to choose,” the second GOP strategist said.

Other Republicans have expressed skepticism that a senator would ultimately win the nomination. Johnson noted that any Republican governors interested in running would need to jump on the national stage sooner rather than later.

“Other than DeSantis, there’s just not a lot of these guys that have a national profile that’s going to be the kind of name recognition you would need to break through,” Johnson said. “They would need a moment very soon where they become the guy or the gal that breaks the mold.”

However, Ford O’Connell, a GOP strategist, said “the calculus doesn’t change.”

“It’s going to be either JD Vance or one of the two Floridians — Marco Rubio or Ron DeSantis,” he said.

“Elections are about name ID and a little bit of swagger,” he added.

articles.title: Trump’s redistricting was meant to save House GOP majority. It backfired
articles.summary: President Trump’s redistricting campaign backfired on House Republicans in spectacular fashion Tuesday, helping Democrats achieve massive gains en route to flipping control of the lower chamber in the next Congress. The rare, mid-decade redistricting push was hardly the only factor challenging Republicans on Election Day, when GOP candidates were dragged down by the volatile economy,…
articles.body:
President Trump’s redistricting campaign backfired on House Republicans in spectacular fashion Tuesday, helping Democrats achieve massive gains en route to flipping control of the lower chamber in the next Congress.

The rare, mid-decade redistricting push was hardly the only factor challenging Republicans on Election Day, when GOP candidates were dragged down by the volatile economy, an unpopular Iran war, and Trump’s dismal approval ratings, which were well underwater as voters went to the polls.

But the new House lines, which were drawn to give Republicans double-digit gains across a number of GOP states, largely flopped in two respects. First, Republicans failed to knock off even a single Democratic incumbent Tuesday, including 10 sitting Democrats who were directly targeted by the new GOP maps.

And second, in some states, the new maps either diluted the conservative vote in traditionally redder districts or forced Republican incumbents to introduce themselves to large numbers of new voters. In both cases, the lines made the terrain more difficult for some Republicans — incumbents and newcomers alike — making seats that were once conservative strongholds more vulnerable to a blue wave like the one that hit Tuesday.

Those trends were most visible in Texas, North Carolina and Ohio, where Democrats kept their incumbents in place while knocking off a number of Republicans who were considered untouchable even the day before.

“Simply put, their gerrymandering scheme absolutely backfired,” Democratic Rep. Suzan DelBene (Wash.), the head of the House Democrats’ campaign arm, told reporters Wednesday. “And it should send a strong message to any Republican thinking of pursuing any more gerrymanders next year: They do so at their own peril, because it’s clear that the American people hate it when politicians pick their voters.”

It wasn’t supposed to turn out that way.

Beginning last year, Trump had pressed Republican-controlled states all across the country to alter their House maps with designs to pad the GOP’s tiny majority and prevent Democrats from seizing power.

No fewer than eight Republican states took up the challenge, redrawing the lines to lend Republicans a new advantage. The campaign was helped by a Supreme Court decision that deemed some Black-majority districts to be unconstitutional — a ruling that freed several red states in the South to adopt new maps eliminating Black-majority districts.

At the height of the GOP’s optimism, the changes were expected to flip 16 Democratic seats.

While the effort paid dividends in several districts by driving some Democrats into early retirement, including Rep. Steve Cohen in Tennessee, Cleo Fields in Louisiana and Lloyd Doggett in Texas, most of the targeted Democrats stayed to fight it out. And all of them won.

That list includes Texas Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez; Florida Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz; Ohio Reps. Marcy Kaptur and Greg Landsman; North Carolina Rep. Don Davis; and Alabama Rep. Shomari Figures.

Florida Rep. Darren Soto also holds a lead despite redistricting, though his race has yet to be called.

In Missouri, Republicans initially thought they’d drawn Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D) out of office. But the new GOP map was blocked by the courts, and Cleaver skated to a 12th term in the district around Kansas City, winning nearly 70 percent of the vote.

“The Democrats did a really good job in retaining their incumbents to run for reelection in those seats,” a GOP campaign strategist acknowledged. “If those are all open seats … virtually no money would be being spent there and it’s kind of an automatic pickup.”

Meanwhile, the new maps helped to undermine some of the GOP candidates in those same states.

In Texas, for instance, where Republicans sought to flip five seats, the new map helped Democrats knock off GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in a district Trump won by 18 points in 2024. Democrats also secured wins in the three other districts that Republicans thought were theirs, including in the 9th District, vacated by Democratic Rep. Al Green.

A similar trend occurred in Ohio, where Democrats not only protected their incumbents in newly redder districts but also picked up three GOP seats, including those held by incumbent Republican Reps. Mike Turner and Max Miller.

In Florida, Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) defended the state’s new map this week, noting that Republicans controlled 20 seats before redistricting and are on track to hold the same number after the midterms.

Still, Florida Republicans had drawn the new lines with designs to pick up four seats, and Democrats won two of the three incumbent races along with the open seat in the 22nd District, as well. And Soto may still hang on to his district, allowing Democrats to go four for four.

In Tennessee, meanwhile, the new lines might help to erase the advantage Republicans gained by eliminating Cohen’s blue seat around Memphis. That’s because GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais is fighting for his political survival in the 4th District after winning there with 70 percent of the vote in 2024.

North Carolina might have been the biggest surprise of them all. Not only did Davis defend his seat in the 1st District, but Democrats were on track Wednesday to pick up as many as six GOP-held seats, including in deep red districts that even Democratic operatives had not foreseen.

Democrats, meanwhile, also posted gains from their own redistricting effort in California, which was launched last year in response to Trump’s campaign.

“We made clear last year, when this corrupt effort to rig the midterm elections by gerrymandering congressional maps in red states all across the country began, that Republicans might start this redistricting and gerrymandering battle, but Democrats were going to finish it,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said Wednesday.

“And last night, that’s exactly what happened.”
