articles.title: Mississippi has an unexpectedly close Senate race but no recount procedure
articles.summary: The Mississippi Senate race could be headed for the courts, as two candidates are locked in a tight contest with no recount procedure on the books. The elect...
articles.body:
The Mississippi Senate race could be headed for the courts, as two candidates are locked in a tight contest with no recount procedure on the books.

The election between Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom remained too close to call as of Wednesday evening, with Colom leading by less than a quarter of a percentage point. That's fewer than 2,000 votes.

And ballots are still coming in. The state allows mail ballots to be counted so long as they were postmarked by Election Day and received up to five business days later, a law that was upheld by the Supreme Court this summer. Mississippi is still waiting to see if roughly 3,600 outstanding ballots show up in time, according to the state's top election official.

In addition to those, Colom's campaign put the count for provisional ballots at around 15,000 on Election Day — but both sides are holding their breath.

"We are going to make sure every single vote has been counted, and I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat," Colom said in a post on the social platform X on election night.

Hyde-Smith assured supporters at a campaign watch party she wasn't going anywhere.

"I'll tell you the Democrats got out and worked, they really got out and worked, and a lot of them showed up today. But not enough of them. I'll just tell you that right now," the senator said, according to Mississippi Today . "I assure you I will continue to be your U.S. senator."

The final margins may well determine what happens next. A wide swing in either direction could soften the chance of legal challenges, but a close result could have the loser's lawyers racing to court.

"In some states, you know, a really close election automatically triggers a recount. That's not true in Mississippi," said Ronald Rychlak, a professor at the University of Mississippi Law School. "In fact, a candidate does not have an automatic right to a recount, even if they offer to pay for it in Mississippi."

State law establishes specific procedures for Mississippi Legislature candidates to contest the election. And if it were a county-level race, for example, state law would give candidates a 20-day window. "The candidate or the party has to go in front of the court and make the case," Rychlak said. "So instead of it being sort of an automatic thing, there is an evidentiary basis that has to be established, and there are procedures in place to help the party gather evidence to make that evidentiary basis."

But when it comes to federal offices like the U.S. Senate, nothing in Mississippi law provides an express way to contest the general election. It effectively leaves it up to judges to determine how disputes are resolved in any push by either side.

"You might not recount every precinct, and maybe a recount is sought in a particular area because that's where the evidence suggests that there may have been mistakes made," Rychlak said. "Then there would be a determination as to whether there was sufficient evidence set forth, and a court at that point could order, you know, a full or partial recount of the votes."

The lack of clarity is an anomaly. Other states have rules for handling challenges to congressional results, but Mississippi's are limited to primaries only.

Chris McDaniel attempted to contest the results of the GOP Senate primary after losing to Thad Cochran in 2014, alleging voter fraud. The state Republican executive committee declined to review the complaint because McDaniel had missed the 20-day cutoff. The Mississippi Supreme Court later agreed .

As Mississippi begins to sort out this year's unexpectedly close race, there's also the question of how Congress itself will react. The Constitution gives each chamber the power to "be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members."

There's another reason the answer may still take time. National Republicans took a Supreme Court loss earlier this year on when mail ballots can be counted, and now the party is grappling with the real-world implications.

In June, the high court ruled 5-4 that federal law does not preempt Mississippi and more than a dozen other states from accepting mail ballots that arrive after Election Day, so long as they were postmarked by then.

Responding to the ruling against the Republican National Committee (RNC), the committee's chair, Joe Gruters, said: "Republicans are not going to be deterred by this decision, and the RNC will keep fighting to have elections end on Election Day as Americans want."

But now, the party may need to rely on those votes to swing back into the lead in Mississippi. Decision Desk HQ estimated that roughly 8,500 ballots were still outstanding as of Wednesday, and many of the remaining ballots will be those last-arriving mail ballots.

Republicans for years attempted to shoot down the practice, which became more widespread in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Adding to the sting was that the Supreme Court's rejection was authored by Justice Amy Coney Barrett, one of President Trump's own appointees. She took on relentless public attacks from conservatives for it.

Although the justice perhaps wasn't envisioning a nail-biter Senate race this year, Barrett conceded at the time it was a "significant concern" that Mississippi's results could give rise to the appearance of fraud if the results "appear to flip after Election Day."

Still, Barrett said that isn't the Supreme Court's problem.

"Election fraud and its appearance are serious issues. Like other such issues, however, they must be addressed through the democratic process," she wrote.

It means that Mississippi is continuing to accept mail ballots through Nov. 10, five business days after polls closed.

"With the vote as close as it [is], that means we're going to have to wait to make sure that those are all in," Rychlak said. "We really have to count every ballot this time, and that means we have to until we have every ballot."

articles.title: How Democrats plan to use their majorities to constrain Trump
articles.summary: Senate and House Democrats are gearing up for a multifront war with President Trump over the next two years, vowing to use their new majorities after Tuesday’s landslide wins to unwind as much of Trump’s agenda as possible and cement his status as a lame-duck president. Ending the war with Iran — which voters blamed…
articles.body:
Senate and House Democrats are gearing up for a multifront war with President Trump over the next two years, vowing to use their new majorities after Tuesday’s landslide wins to unwind as much of Trump’s agenda as possible and cement his status as a lame-duck president.

Ending the war with Iran — which voters blamed for higher gas, diesel and grocery prices — is high atop the list, and Democratic leaders now have new leverage to block funding for the Defense Department and to pressure Trump to bring the conflict to a quick close.

Reversing the Republican cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) enacted by Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act and reviving the generous health insurance premium subsidies that lapsed at the start of this year are other top priorities.

They plan to stop what they say is the Trump administration’s overzealous enforcement of immigration laws, which they believe helped push many Hispanic voters to cast ballots for Democrats, and end what they’re calling his “weaponization” of the Justice Department.

And Senate Democrats warn that Trump will need to advance judicial nominees with very different backgrounds and records than the nominees he’s been sending to Capitol Hill over the past 20 months if he wants to add new judges to the federal bench.

Democrats expect to control between 54-56 Senate seats next year and at least 255 seats in the lower chamber, giving them the largest House majority of any party since former President Obama’s landslide victory in the 2008 election.

“First, Americans want Washington to bring down the cost of living,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) told reporters during a press conference Wednesday at the Senate Democratic campaign headquarters.

“Second, Americans want us to clean up corruption in government. They know that Trump is the most corrupt president in American history. No American should have to make trade-offs at the supermarket while Trump is making insider trades on the stock market.

“And third, they want us to check Donald Trump’s chaos at home and abroad,” he continued, alluding to the shooting deaths of two anti-immigration protesters earlier this year. “We’ve seen too many Americans die on our streets and in uniform overseas because of Trump’s erratic judgment. The American people don’t know what the heck we’re fighting for in Iran.

“This war must end,” Schumer declared. “It must end.”

Schumer on Wednesday noted “we have some Republicans who have joined us already on ending the war,” referring to the four GOP senators who have supported a war powers resolution to immediately end the conflict.

And he said Democrats could also exercise “the power of the purse” to restrain Trump’s authority as commander in chief.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), who is poised to become the next Speaker, pledged, “We’re going to get out of the gate fast.”

He said that House Democrats would “have a conversation as a caucus” when lawmakers reconvene in Washington next week for a lame-duck session.

House Democrats plan to bring to the floor bills to revive the expanded health insurance premium subsidies under the Affordable Care Act, which lapsed at the start of 2026, along with legislation to reverse the Medicaid cuts Republicans enacted last year.

“We need to reverse the Medicaid cuts, we need to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, we need to end this reckless and costly war of choice that has skyrocketed gas prices all across the country, and we need to stop the Trump tariffs,” Jeffries announced.

Schumer warned Wednesday that Trump’s judicial nominees will face a very tough road and urged the president to pick nominees with strong credentials and track records that Democrats could support.

“We want judicial nominees like we showed in ’23 and ’24, who obey the law, who have fidelity to the rule of law,” he said, referring to nominees advanced by former President Biden. “Too many of Trump’s nominees did not have that at all.”

Schumer and Jeffries may face a difficult task in unifying their new majorities given that many Democrats are seeking to inflict retribution against Trump by investigating his family’s business dealings and what they believe were efforts by the Justice Department to shield the president from the fallout of the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia (Calif.), the incoming House Oversight and Government Reform Committee chair, fired off a warning to the Trump administration Tuesday evening, advising them in a terse statement to “lawyer up.”

And Democrats are looking to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth if Trump doesn’t remove him from his post.

House Democrats have already filed articles of impeachment against Hegseth as well as Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Education Secretary Linda McMahon.

Senate Democrats are also threatening investigations into the Trump administration over issues ranging from what they say is the weaponization of the Justice Department, to what they allege is influence peddling within the administration, to the explosive increase in Trump’s net worth since taking office in January 2025.

“Make no mistake, whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court, entangle him in legislative razor wire,” Schumer pledged. “The days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over.”

But Schumer and Jeffries are worried the new Democratic majorities could become too consumed by partisan investigations and lose sight of the affordability issue that motivated millions of voters to support Democratic candidates, including in deep-red states such as Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

“There was such rampant corruption there has to be some investigations, but we’re not going to take our eye off the ball. Number one: Reducing costs, ending corruption,” Schumer said.

Both leaders have downplayed moving immediately to impeach Hegseth, giving Trump some space to find a new Pentagon chief without it looking like a capitulation to Democrats.

Trump on Wednesday floated the possibility that Hegseth would make a good Republican senator from Tennessee if he were appointed to fill the remaining term of Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R), who won election to become Tennessee’s next governor.

Trump told reporters that he’s not considering removing Hegseth from his job but observed he would make a “very popular” senator if he replaced Blackburn.

Schumer downplayed the prospect of impeachment proceedings and a Senate trial for Hegseth.

“Everyone will make their own interpretation of [what’s ahead] in terms of Hegseth,” he said.

Jeffries only quipped: “Is Pete Hegseth still around?”

But some Republicans in both chambers also want Hegseth to step down.

Retiring Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) indicated on social media that he plans to push for vote on articles of impeachment against Hegseth in the lame-duck Congress.

And retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) told CBS News that Hegseth might have to step down to secure funding for the Defense Department.

“Hegseth has a reckoning,” Tillis said. “He is one of the reasons why we don’t have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need.”

“I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he’s the best person to bring those needs to Congress. If he wants something done before the end of this Congress, which is only 60 days away,” he warned.

articles.title: Iran, Gaza, Ukraine: What will US midterm results mean for these conflicts?
articles.summary: Despite wins, Democrats lack the two-thirds majority needed to overturn a presidential veto and push through a law.
articles.body:
As Democrats swept to victory in a blue wave across the United States in this week’s midterm elections, the world’s eyes turned to Congress and how it is likely to address conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Ukraine from January.

The midterms have largely been viewed as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s policies, particularly his decision to start a war with Iran in February.

The war has proved deeply unpopular in the US, as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused fuel prices to soar, and as it has cost US taxpayers an estimated $47bn so far. Several prominent Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have already made moves to distance themselves from the conflict .

European leaders cautiously welcomed the results on Wednesday, voicing hopes that the Democrat-led lawmakers taking office in January would help mend fractured transatlantic ties and boost Washington’s waning support for Ukraine amid Russia’s invasion. Trump has withdrawn support for Ukraine, blaming strikes on Russian oil facilities for the fuel crisis, calling for the resignation of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and suspending sanctions on Russian oil.

As well as largely supporting Ukraine, Democrats have also been strongly opposed to the US war on Iran since it began, unlike the Trump administration. While the previous Biden administration did little to deter Israel in its genocidal war on Gaza, a new wave of progressive Democrats elected to office in the midterms has loudly opposed it, as well as the pogroms against Palestinian communities by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

On Tuesday, as defeats to Republican candidates flooded in, Trump promised to use his presidential veto power to push back against any “insane” policies from Democrats in Congress. Presidential vetoes can only be overturned by a two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress.

So what’s likely to change and what does this mean for conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Ukraine? Here’s what we know:

Republicans suffered a crushing defeat on Tuesday, losing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate to the Democrats, including in some traditionally conservative states like Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and others which backed Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

In the 100-seat Senate, Democrats now have 54 seats while Republicans have 44, with two more to be declared. In the House of Representatives, Democrats have won 242 seats, well above the 218 threshold needed to control the chamber, while Republicans have won 151 seats.

Democrats have governors in 28 states, compared with the Republicans’ 20, with two yet to be declared.

There were many firsts for the Democrats : Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan became the first Muslim senator; Georgia voted in Keisha Lance Bottoms as the first Black female governor; Gina Hinojosa became the first Latina governor in Texas, and in New Mexico, Deb Haaland became the first female Native American governor.

The US-Israel war on Iran was top of voters’ minds in this election. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump admitted it had contributed largely to the Republicans’ spectacular losses but maintained it was worth it.

It “drove the price of gasoline up a little bit short term … but at the same time if I had to do it again I’d have to do it again because long term it’s the only answer – you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he told reporters.

Trump had campaigned for the presidency on promises to end US involvement in foreign wars and to lower the cost of living.

Since he took office in January 2025, Trump has dragged the US into two wars on Iran without seeking Congress’s approval. Democrats attempted to push back with little success, as Trump relied heavily on executive orders to bypass them. Popular anger at his administration is clear in his plunging ratings. On the eve of the election, only 32 percent of respondents said they approved of Trump’s policies, a Reuters/Ipsos poll suggested.

Still, Trump has kept the option of further strikes on Iran, as well as diplomatic talks, open. He has also threatened to use his veto powers to frustrate Democrats.

Democrat Senator Chuck Schumer told reporters on Wednesday that lawmakers have the financial upper hand.

“We are going to end the war … the founding fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people.”

However, although a Democrat-led Congress may well control the purse strings, restricting funding for the war may not be straightforward.

James Boys, research fellow at the Centre on US Politics at University College London, told Al Jazeera on Wednesday: “With troops in theatre, this would prove to be highly problematic and be seen to be placing American lives at risk.”

Analysts also said the War Powers Resolution is unlikely to succeed in reining Trump in. Previous attempts to use the 1973 federal law have been defeated or rendered ineffective.

The War Powers Resolution states that a president can repel an imminent attack, but military actions must end within 60 days unless Congress declares war. The president can then issue a veto, which can only be overturned by a two-thirds supermajority in both the House and Senate, something the Democrats do not have.

Iran may now press harder for the US to agree to its conditions for ending the war, given the weakening of the Republican Party in this election.

Will the Republicans’ losses affect Gaza?

Democrats have long been known for their pro-Israel stance. Former President Joe Biden’s administration continued military support for Israel after it launched its war on Gaza in October 2023, even as thousands of Palestinians were being slaughtered in Gaza.

But several so-called “progressive” Democratic candidates elected on Tuesday stood out for their criticism of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the illegal Israeli settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, and the US’s longstanding unwavering financial and military support for Israel.

Abdul El-Sayed, who won a seat in the Senate for Michigan on Tuesday despite a vicious campaign against him by Republicans and the pro-Israel AIPAC super PAC , railed against the Trump administration and pledged to press for the withdrawal of US aid to Israel.

In an apparent attempt to appease voters on election day, Trump announced on Fox News that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had suggested the US should cease its $4bn annual aid to the country.

“We’ve ⁠⁠already agreed that ⁠⁠by the end of this year we won’t be paying Israel,” he said, adding that “we’ll help Israel if they need it.”

Trump came to power promising to end the Russia-Ukraine war in “days”. He has failed to do this, however, and has increasingly turned his ire on Ukraine and its European allies, who he says should be bearing the brunt of financial and military support. Earlier this year, Trump appeared to suggest that Ukraine should give up territory already seized by Russia in order to end the war and get a peace deal in place.

Last February, when Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited the White House , Trump called the Ukrainian president “ungrateful” in a heated exchange.

Most recently, Trump has blamed Zelenskyy for causing the rise in global diesel prices, which have badly affected farmers and truckers in the US, by striking Russian oil facilities. He also suspended sanctions on Russian oil, which were passed in September following bipartisan support in Congress, causing anger from within his own Republican Party.

During recent strikes by Russia on Kyiv, Ukraine accused the US of withholding intelligence about incoming missiles and restricting Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite network owned by Elon Musk, which it uses to guide its missiles.

Trump’s administration has also delayed the transfer of weapons Ukraine says it desperately needs, while Trump has called for Zelenskyy to step down as president, claiming Ukraine “does not want to end this war”. Washington, in October, waived sanctions on Russia and began buying Russian oil, alarming European leaders and drawing rebuke from Ukraine.

All of this is a complete change since the previous Biden administration, which promised Washington “will not walk away” from Ukraine.

Now, Ukraine hopes it will be back on the agenda in January when the new Congress convenes.

“The Democrats speak very clearly about supporting Ukraine and providing assistance to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy told German broadcaster ZDF. “They speak about renewing the connection between the United States and Europe … Therefore, there is hope that a balance of power will emerge, and that we will receive more support.”

Iranians carry their country’s giant national flag during a rally in front of the former US embassy to mark the anniversary of the 1979 Iran hostage crisis, in Tehran, on November 4, 2026. In 1979, 52 embassy staff were held hostage for 444 days by Iranian students, who demanded that Washington hand over Iran’s recently toppled shah [Atta Kenare/AFP]

articles.title: ‘Knives out’: Will Congress impeach Pete Hegseth after GOP midterms loss?
articles.summary: Democrats can adopt the impeachment articles in the House but will need Republican backing in the Senate.
articles.body:
The Republican Party’s stunning defeat in the United States midterm elections on Tuesday has prompted calls from within the Trump administration and from its critics for accountability over a focus of voter discontent: the US-Israel war on Iran.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appears to have emerged as a central target of those demands since the Democrats’ sweeping victory , in which they won control of both chambers of Congress.

Some Republican lawmakers and other critics have argued that the Pentagon chief played a leading role in convincing US President Donald Trump to attack Iran with no exit strategy.

On Wednesday, Congressman Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky who has repeatedly locked horns with Trump and his aides, called on Hegseth to resign. An impeachment vote in the House could come as soon as next week.

If that happens, Hegseth’s fate would be decided by a Congress still dominated by the Republicans, with new members elected this week only taking office in January. But some reports suggest that Republican lawmakers are increasingly inclined to push Hegseth out of the Pentagon.

Trump, who has described the defense secretary as a champion of the Iran war, told reporters on Wednesday that he was not considering replacing him. “I think he’s doing a very good job,” the president said.

The Republican congressman filed eight impeachment accusations in September against Hegseth.

In an interview with CNN, he said he plans to trigger a vote when Congress returns next week. The US news outlet said multiple Republican sources said they expect it to pass.

Massie lost his Republican House primary in May and only has the current session of Congress to pursue the impeachment.

He argued that Hegseth’s “constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran.”

“He is abusing the power of his office to ignore congressional war powers resolutions, to kidnap foreign leaders and to intimidate critics of the Trump administration by retaliating against them for exercising free speech,” Massie said.

In January, the US abducted then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, and brought them to New York to face trial on charges including drug trafficking — accusations they deny. Venezuela has since effectively been a US protectorate, with its economy and unmatched oil reserves controlled from Washington.

Massie, who lost to a primary challenger backed by the president, has long been at odds with Trump.

Aside from being critical of the war on Iran, he has denounced the president’s military support for Israel, pushed for the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files and voted against Trump’s signature tax legislation.

Many Republicans remain unwilling to directly blame Trump for the midterm defeat, yet they recognise the war in Iran as the main reason for the electoral wipeout.

While not pinning blame on anyone, Vice President JD Vance conceded that “the reason we lost is the war.”

“Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” he said.

Hegseth, one of the biggest proponents of military action in Iran, is seen by many as having played a pivotal role in convincing the president to enter a conflict that worsened the affordability crisis and consumed expensive US munitions.

“You can already see the knives out for Secretary Hegseth,” Paul Musgrave, an associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera.

Republican Senator Thom Tillis said Hegseth would face “a reckoning” in the post-election “lame duck” Congress and claimed Trump would not be able to get the necessary Pentagon funding if he remains in his job.

“I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he’s the best person to bring those needs to Congress, if he wants something done before the end of this Congress, which is only 60 days away,” the North Carolina senator said, according to US media.

Tillis, who in January 2025 backed Hegseth’s confirmation, said that vote was the “biggest regret of my career”. Last month, he urged Trump to fire him for his “inept management of the brave men”.

CNN quoted Republican Party sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, who said that Hegseth oversold US ability to overpower Iran and continued to advocate for escalation, even when it was clear that military force would not bring Tehran’s government to surrender.

Can an impeachment vote succeed in Congress?

An impeachment vote needs only a simple majority to pass in the House of Representatives. The Democrats currently have 214 members in the chamber, and would need just a few Republicans to back Massie’s motion to reach the 218 votes needed to secure a majority.

If the vote takes place after the new House takes shape in January, Democrats will not need any Republican support: The party is on track to amass the largest majority since at least the 2008 election, with 240 seats confirmed so far and more on the way.

But an impeachment in the House would need to be approved by a two-thirds majority in the Senate to force Hegseth out.

The Democrats are currently in a minority in the Senate, and even in the new Congress, will have a maximum of 56 seats out of 100. That means they would need at least 11 Republicans to join them to secure the 67 votes needed for the two-thirds majority.

That threshold explains why Trump, twice impeached by the House, was acquitted by the Senate in both cases. That is also why the only two cabinet secretaries ever impeached by the House — William Belknap in 1876 and Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024 — were both subsequently acquitted by the Senate.

Why pressure on Hegseth to quit might grow

But analysts say that regardless of what happens with the Massie impeachment motion, pressure on Hegseth to quit will likely grow — including from within the Republican Party.

Richard Johnson, a senior lecturer in politics at the Queen Mary University of London, said the poor Republican showing in the midterms may push those with party leadership ambitions to eventually portray themselves as “more MAGA than Trump”. Ending and avoiding foreign wars has been a central pillar of the Make America Great Again movement that Trump built.

Such candidates would argue that Trump and his inner circle had succumbed to the US “deep state” on the question of Iran, Johnson said, “betraying the promise of no new wars and pushing up the cost of living for ordinary Americans”.

As a result, Johnson added, Republicans may not opt for a more “establishment” candidate going forward but for a more anti-establishment choice.

In the meantime, they might seek to distance themselves from the war — as Vance is already trying to do.

US President Donald Trump conceded the Iran war was the defining issue that drove a Republican pummeling in midterm elections, though analysts were skeptical that any long-term truce was on the horizon. Yet Trump nevertheless insisted that "if I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again ," and one leading expert said the oil selloff " has been somewhat baffling ," arguing that "the risk of escalation structurally grows post midterms, and the outcome (a Dem victory) has been the base case for months."

articles.title: US trade policy unlikely to shift despite midterm defeat
articles.summary: “Trump will reject any attempt to limit the use of his favorite tool,” an Atlantic Council scholar argued.
articles.body:
US tariffs were a drag on Republicans in midterm elections, but President Donald Trump is unlikely to change tack on trade, experts said. Trump has sought to use tariffs to bolster domestic employment and cut trade deficits, but "each of these goals is wrong-headed, and neither has been met ," one analyst wrote in the Financial Times.

The legislature has limited sway over the imposition of levies , a former Trump administration economic adviser noted, and even if it sought to force his hand, " Trump will reject any attempt to limit the use of his favorite tool ," an Atlantic Council scholar argued. One country has benefited, though: Canada's prime minister said the US is "asking less" and "offering more" in once-rancorous negotiations.

articles.title: Iran is the biggest winner of Tuesday’s election
articles.summary: Iran is the biggest winner of Tuesday’s election — or at least, that is what Tehran will likely conclude. Recall that last month, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Gen. Hossein Mohebbi, in a 25-page letter to the “Honorable People of the United States of America,” encouraged “Americans to vote against President Trump ahead of the midterm elections to change U.S. policy toward Tehran…
articles.body:
Iran is the biggest winner of Tuesday’s election — or at least, that is what Tehran will likely conclude.

Recall that last month, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Gen. Hossein Mohebbi, in a 25-page letter to the “Honorable People of the United States of America,” encouraged “Americans to vote against President Trump ahead of the midterm elections to change U.S. policy toward Tehran and accept the offer of a “peaceful coexistence.”

They did. Iran got the regime change they wanted. What happened? As the saying goes, “ American’s love a winner .” For whatever reason, Trump took on Iran but failed to deliver a decisive blow, opting instead to play for the tie and make “a deal,” as he likes to say.

Trump told the American public that the war with Iran — Operation Epic Fury — would “last four to five weeks but could “go far longer than that.”

Epic Fury lasted just 38 days — a little over five weeks.

Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and many of the regime’s senior leaders were killed in the opening airstrike. The assumption was that the regime would collapse and the Iranian people would eventually rise up and “ take over [their] government .”

But it did not collapse. The regime remained in power, thanks in part to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Basij paramilitary. Regime survival was their mantra. When Trump demanded Iran’s “ unconditional surrender ,” they dug in deeper. Forty-seven years of autocratic theocracy and indoctrination provided the foundation for their resistance.

Trump told us his objectives had been achieved: “obliterate Iran’s ballistic missile arsenal and production capability, annihilate its navy, sever its support for terrorist proxies and ensure the world’s leading state sponsor of terrorism never acquires a nuclear weapon.”

Conventionally, Tehran was defeated. The U.S. destroyed Iran’s Navy and Air Force , along with its nuclear threat capability. Iran’s anti-aircraft systems and missile-building capabilities were largely knocked out as well.

As important as that is, the regime has remained in power and continued to exert influence over what it could control: the price of oil.

Initially, Iran was able to shut down the Strait of Hormuz and attacked oil refineries in neighboring Gulf nation states. Then they leveraged their proxies — Houthi rebels in Yemen and Shia militias in Iraq — to attack Saudi Arabia’s oil refineries and their East-West pipeline. Houthi rebels would later threaten shipping at other key choke-points — the Red Sea, the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the Gulf of Aden.

Asymmetrically they were still in the fight. And as the White House would have to learn, air power alone was not going to defeat the regime — something more than a century of military aviation should have already made clear.

Trump’s forever cease-fire was initiated on April 7. It has now reached 212 days — 30 weeks. It provided Iran the breathing room it needed to maneuver and played to its strength, which is negotiations.

With the assistance of mediators from Pakistan and Qatar, Tehran simply outplayed the Trump negotiation team of Vice President J.D. Vance, Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner. The Iranians dragged the non-shooting war out to election day, driving up the cost of oil and diesel and shifting the burden onto American voters where they could least afford it — their pocket books.

By the time the White House had shifted its primary effort from the military instrument of national power to the economic instrument, they were running short on time.

As successful as Operation Economic Outcast was, it was implemented too late to bring the war to a close prior to the election, even if we did help Gulf partners get 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil while preventing Iran with a blockade from exporting its own oil.

Iran raised the cost of doing business for the Trump administration — specifically, the cost of insurance and military escorts. For the White House and Iran, the finish line was Nov. 3. Iran outlasted Washington. But the regime, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described as, “run by lunatics — religious fanatic lunatics” with “an ambition to have nuclear weapons” is still in power.

So what’s the plan now? Walking away from Iran and allowing the regime to remain in power cannot be the end state. It simply trades out a forever cease-fire for forever instability in the region.

The solution begins with addressing Iran’s leverage over the Strait of Hormuz. Two critical elements must be achieved: Secure the strait and remove the regime from power.

The U.S. has control of the strait but has not secured it. The U.S. has weakened the regime, but has not removed it from power. Iran will likely use the outcome of Tuesday’s elections to harden its negotiating position and save its nuclear weapons program in the process.

Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: Inside Trump's fight against cartels: White House official details Homeland Security Task Force crackdowns
articles.summary: President Trump receives photos of drug seizures during briefings and presses officials on protecting individual victims amid the sweeping cartel crackdown.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: President Donald Trump may be briefed on sprawling cartel networks and massive drug seizures, but sometimes it's the story of a single American crime victim that captures his attention, a White House official told Fox News Digital. The official described how Trump can shift from discussions about major criminal organizations to an individual harmed by crime, pressing officials about what more the federal government can do to protect everyday Americans. "I could be talking about very grand cartel stuff, which he's very interested in," the official said, explaining that the president may instead focus on one person hurt by criminal activity. WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES The official said Trump receives regular briefings that include photographs of narcotics seized by federal agents. While the president takes pride in successful enforcement operations, the official described his reaction as quickly turning to the amount of work still ahead. The president's response to the photographs, according to the official, is to ask what more can be done to stop the flow of drugs into American communities. Trump also pressed for federal agencies to work together as the administration seeks to dismantle entire criminal organizations rather than simply arrest their leaders as agencies have done in the past. That approach is at the center of a campaign that has brought together more than 20 federal agencies under the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative. According to figures provided by the White House, the task forces made nearly 12,000 arrests during fiscal year 2026, seized approximately 161 metric tons of drugs, $482 million in criminal assets and nearly 13,000 weapons. ICE ARRESTS MORE THAN 100 ALLEGED GANG MEMBERS IN SINGLE WEEK, INCLUDING VIOLENT MS-13, TDA SUSPECTS: DHS The administration also reported 676 criminal organizations disrupted in figures provided to Fox News Digital. The task forces have 6,585 active investigations, including more than 1,000 targeting major drug kingpins and 814 targeting designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations. The task force operates nationwide, bringing together federal law enforcement agencies with hundreds of state, local and international partners. Its public website, HSTF.gov, outlines the initiative's mission, participating agencies and enforcement efforts targeting cartels, transnational gangs and other criminal organizations. Behind those numbers, the official described an effort to break down longstanding divisions among federal law enforcement agencies that previously pursued overlapping investigations with varying degrees of cooperation. DOJ TOUTS HUNDREDS OF GUN, DRUG ARRESTS AS ST LOUIS SURGE OPERATION ENDS: 'VIOLENCE IS NOT INEVITABLE' The official said more than 1,800 cartel-related narcotics task forces previously operated across the country, with varying degrees of coordination. Agencies including the FBI, DEA and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) could pursue overlapping targets, occasionally competing to bring indictments first. Interagency disagreements sometimes left investigations stalled for years, the official said. Under the new approach, the National Coordination Center brings together the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security, with support from military and intelligence partners, to resolve conflicts and coordinate investigations across jurisdictions. DRUG CARTEL KINGPIN AMONG TARGETS IN SWEEPING TRUMP CRACKDOWN ON ALLEGED MEXICAN CORRUPTION NETWORK "Now we're all indicting together," the official said. Rather than focusing exclusively on high-value targets, investigators are pursuing the transportation networks, distributors, collectors and money launderers that keep criminal enterprises operating. The official explained that taking down a cartel leader does not necessarily dismantle the organization because others can quickly assume leadership. "There's five more people ready to step up as soon as we take out one," the official said. A sweeping federal investigation into the Trinitarios gang in Massachusetts illustrates the kind of coordinated law enforcement effort the administration is pursuing. In June, federal prosecutors announced racketeering conspiracy charges against 26 alleged gang leaders, members and associates in connection with five murders and 19 attempted murders. The announcement brought the total number of Trinitarios members charged in related investigations over two years to 56. Prosecutors alleged the gang's involvement in 11 murders and 30 attempted murders since 2017. Court documents describe chapters operating in the Boston area whose members allegedly engaged in drug trafficking, kidnappings and witness intimidation. Investigators also alleged the gang recruited minors attending local schools, sometimes using younger members to conceal weapons or serve as lookouts. The investigation involved HSI, the FBI, DEA, ATF and state and local law enforcement partners. The investigation began before the HSTF initiative, and the charges remain allegations against defendants who have not been convicted. The task force's reach also extends to drug trafficking operations moving narcotics across state lines. In Louisiana, federal prosecutors announced five cases involving more than a dozen defendants and hundreds of kilograms of narcotics. Near Breaux Bridge, investigators discovered approximately 147 kilograms of methamphetamine concealed inside modified ice cream freezers. In another case near Lafayette, authorities found approximately 100 kilograms of cocaine hidden inside an 18-wheeler's cab. The White House official also pointed to Tren de Aragua, the Venezuelan criminal organization that drew national attention during the 2024 presidential campaign, as an example of the administration's broader strategy. Fox News Digital extensively covered allegations of Tren de Aragua activity at apartment complexes in Aurora, Colorado, including accounts from local officials and residents who described violence and intimidation. Trump subsequently made Aurora a recurring focus of his criticism of the Biden administration's border policies. The official recalled Fox News Digital's reporting on the controversy and argued that the administration's coordinated enforcement campaign has weakened the gang's ability to operate openly in the United States. "I'm not saying they're completely gone here, but they are so on their heels because we have this concerted effort taken," the official said. "You don't see them bragging in the social media anymore," the official added. In May, the Justice Department announced charges against more than 25 defendants in a nationwide Tren de Aragua crackdown spanning six federal judicial districts. Authorities reported seizing more than 80 firearms, approximately 18 kilograms of narcotics and more than $100,000. The official described the crackdown as an example of the administration's effort to pursue criminal organizations at multiple levels, rather than concentrating solely on their leaders. The administration is seeking to apply that same approach to more deeply established criminal networks, including the notorious Sinaloa Cartel. The official said the task force's ultimate objective is not simply accumulating arrests or celebrating drug seizures, but reducing the ability of criminal organizations to threaten Americans. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For Trump, the official said, even major seizures can serve as reminders of the work still ahead. The president may take pride in enforcement results, but the official described his attention as quickly turning to how much more needs to be done to stop narcotics from reaching American communities.

articles.title: Midterms force a reckoning on Iran war
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ How the midterms affect the Iran war ▪ Johnson to stand down as leader ▪ Outstanding Alaska, Mississippi ballots ▪ GOP gerrymandering backfires The Democratic sweep that stunned much of Washington on Tuesday night could drastically shorten President Trump’s runway to end the war in Iran, which even he conceded was…
articles.body:
▪ Outstanding Alaska, Mississippi ballots

The Democratic sweep that stunned much of Washington on Tuesday night could drastically shorten President Trump ’s runway to end the war in Iran, which even he conceded was a driving force in the election blowout.

When Democrats take control of the House and Senate in January, they will have new leverage over Pentagon spending, and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) made clear that his party intends to use it.

“We are going to end the war,” Schumer said at a press conference.

“We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people, ” he continued.

The Trump administration has asked Congress for a $1.5 trillion defense budget for next year, including additional Pentagon spending through reconciliation. It has separately requested emergency funding to cover costs tied to the Iran war.

Some Republican lawmakers have reportedly begun talking about a year-end reconciliation bill that could include funding for the Iran war and several other GOP priorities.

That process could allow Republicans to approve the money without Democratic votes, but they have only a few weeks in session to agree on a package and get it through both chambers. They also have to address the Dec. 11 government funding deadline.

It’s unclear how many Republican lawmakers are willing to vote for more war funding after Tuesday’s losses. Both Trump and Vice President Vance said the war hurt their party at the polls.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote on social media. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay.”

“But everyone knows why we lost,” he added. “And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Trump did just that. He said he agreed with the vice president’s assessment but said he doesn’t regret getting involved in the war.

“I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term, and probably — that’s probably, it’s true,” Trump told reporters about Vance’s comments, during an event celebrating his White House ballroom. “But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”

Democrats could also demand accountability from the administration by bringing another war powers resolution. In June, both chambers adopted a concurrent resolution directing Trump to halt unauthorized military activity against Iran, but concurrent resolutions don’t get sent to the president’s desk, and the White House dismissed it as not having force of law.

Democrats this time could pass a joint resolution and send it to Trump for a signature. But if he vetoed the measure, it would take two-thirds of both chambers to override his decision. Even with their new majorities and growing unease over the war among some Republicans, Democrats would need substantial GOP support to override a veto.

Democrats have also indicated they intend to scrutinize the Pentagon and its chief, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth . Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, told Axios that Hegseth “will be forced to answer” for his “chaotic and incompetent leadership.”

He could face punitive measures even before Democrats take control, as Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is promising an impeachment vote when Congress returns this month, unless the Pentagon chief resigns first.

The shifting winds in Washington come as Trump weighs his next step on Iran, with The Hill reporting earlier this week that the president could be leaning toward resuming military activity in Iran over efforts to renew peace talks.

Iranian officials have cast the midterm results as a rejection of the war, but they are still bracing for Trump’s next move, warning the U.S. against more strikes but saying they are prepared to respond if necessary.

“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and ‌we endorse this message,” Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf , Iran’s chief negotiator, wrote in a post on X.

Alexander Bolton has a new piece out for The Hill Insider on how Schumer and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) are already planning to use their majorities to constrain Trump’s agenda. High on that list, he reports, is the Iran war, which voters blame for high gas, diesel and grocery prices.

Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman is projected to defeat Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass to become the next leader of the country’s second-largest city, according to Decision Desk HQ . Raman leads by a narrow 3 points. She will be the city’s first democratic socialist mayor, though she campaigned on being independent from the Democratic Socialists of America.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the Trump administration will continue with deportations following Democrats’ victories in the House and Senate. Mullin has pushed back on critics’ attacks on the administration’s strict crackdown while leading the department.

An appeals court ruled in favor of New York City Zohran Mamdani’s (D) pied-à-terre tax, reversing a lower court decision . The tax would implement an annual surcharge on certain second homes worth more than $5 million and is intended to help narrow the city’s budget deficit.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) looks on as President Trump speaks with reporters, Nov. 1, 2026, at Dubuque Regional Airport in Dubuque, Iowa, en route to a campaign rally. (Jacquelyn Martin, Associated Press)

NEXT MAN UP : House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told his staff on a call Wednesday that he will not run for minority leader after the GOP lost the House, clearing the way for a potentially bitter fight over the party’s future.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) are both expected to launch bids for the role, The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi reports. The contest seems likely to pit the establishment (Scalise) against a more conservative wing of the conference (Jordan).

Trump didn’t pick sides when asked about the race to replace Johnson on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger (R-Texas) is running against House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) for the position of minority whip. Pfluger argued in a letter to his colleagues Wednesday that “new fresh ideas” and a leadership team with a plan to win back the majority in 2028 is needed.

Kochi notes that Johnson and Emmer’s tenures in their leadership positions have been marked by deep divisions within the GOP conference, including some times when conservative hard-liners blocked legislation from advancing to the floor.

▪ The Hill : Republicans sort through election carnage for a message in new era.

▪ The Hill : GOP House incumbents swept away in blue wave.

WAITING GAME : Democrats are assured of a comfortable Senate majority in the next session of Congress, but two key states remain uncalled.

Democrat Mary Peltola narrowly leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in Alaska’s Senate race but is short of the majority she would need to avoid going to ranked-choice tabulation. Presuming that remains the case, that would mean that a couple more weeks could be needed before a winner is declared.

The true surprise nailbiter is Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) trails Democrat Scott Colom by just under 2,000 votes. Ballots are still coming in, and the state allows mail-in ballots to be counted as long as they’re postmarked by Election Day and received within five business days later.

The exact number of outstanding ballots is unknown. A close final result could land the contest in court, but as The Hill’s Sophie Brams and Zach Schonfeld note , Mississippi doesn’t have any law that provides for a recount in federal elections.

That essentially leaves it up to judges to determine how to resolve disputes.

▪ The Hill : Democrats’ success boosts ranks of Hispanic caucus.

MARKET RALLY : The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged 1,569 points, or 3 percent, yesterday in its best post-midterm elections day since 1982, CNN reported, citing data from CFRA Research. Wednesday also marked the Dow’s largest gain since April 2025.

The S&P 500 rose 1.58 percent, in its second-biggest post-midterm gain since 1982. And the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.44 percent, in its biggest post-midterm gain since 2018.

A certain amount of stability that’s expected to come may be the cause.

“Wall Street loves divided government, because typically divided government doesn’t do anything, and it’s very much the case in this particular situation that it’s going to be very hard to do anything affirmative during the last two years of Trump’s administration,” Daniel Alpert , the executive chair at Westwood Capital, told The Hill’s Max Rego .

Oil prices also dropped sharply yesterday as bond yields fell, and investors weighed what the election results might mean for the future of the Iran war. Brent crude fell 8.7 percent to $94.62 a barrel, its lowest close in more than two months. Defense firms’ stocks also fell, with Lockheed Martin down nearly 7 percent.

The Senate will meet at 10:30 a.m. for a pro forma session.

An advertisement for prediction market platform Kalshi hangs at 13th and L Streets in northwest Washington, April 1, 2026. (Allison Robbert, Associated Press)

SPOT ON: Online prediction market platforms were able to predict with remarkable accuracy the outcomes of many midterm races Tuesday, often hours before the races were called by major TV networks, The Hill’s Julia Shapero and Dominick Mastrangelo report .

Despite the growing scrutiny prediction markets have faced on Capitol Hill, traders poured billions of dollars into platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi ahead of the election, gauging with striking accuracy the public’s perception of likely outcomes.

Kalshi said its markets had correctly predicted 98 percent of House, Senate, governor, attorney general, lieutenant governor and secretary of State races. Polymarket similarly said its midterm markets were accurate in 98.4 percent of resolved races, compared with the day before the election.

In many ways, the popularity of prediction markets has the potential to change the way people wait for results to come in.

“It’s now routinely hours between when prediction markets call it versus the TV networks,” Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan wrote in a post on social platform X. “The networks hold out until absolute certainty, and the suspense keeps it entertaining all night. No knock to them, but now there’s Polymarket, and many people are realizing they want to know what’s happening in real time.”

Ross Dahlke , an expert in computational social sciences and a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, noted prediction markets “seem to be highly accurate.”

“The markets just react so quickly to new information in a way that a lot of traditional media isn’t set up to do, particularly with their concern over accuracy, fact-checking — for better or for worse,” he told The Hill.

Pre-election polls similarly had a good night on Tuesday, having mostly projected Democratic gains, but they failed to capture the scale of the party’s sweeping victory. Morning Report’s Jared Gans talked to pollsters for a piece in The Hill Insider on why polls underestimated Democrats.

Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) speaks at the Republican convention on Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas. (Alex Brandon, Associated Press)

DUMMYMANDER DOMINOES : North Carolina Republicans’ decision to redraw the state’s congressional lines has officially backfired as Democrats flipped multiple Republican-held seats that weren’t even on most observers’ radars.

Decision Desk HQ projected Wednesday that GOP Reps. Richard Hudson , Brad Knott , Addison McDowall and Tim Moore will lose their seats to Democratic challengers. That’s in addition to an open seat being vacated by GOP Rep. Chuck Edwards that Democrats also flipped.

Hudson’s loss is particularly notable as he serves as the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, the House GOP’s campaign arm.

Rep. Virginia Foxx is trying to hang on for another term, currently trailing Democrat Chuck Hubbard by less than 100 votes as counting continues.

Republicans in the state legislature pushed through a redistricting plan earlier this year to boost their odds at ousting Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.), whom they have targeted for the past few cycles. Not only did Davis manage to hold on, but the GOP’s plan also ended up backfiring by watering down the party’s majority in redder districts.

Thanks in part to what’s being called the “dummymander,” Democrats will hold a majority of the state’s House seats for the first time in more than a decade.

This effect was arguably most pronounced in North Carolina but happened to some extent in other states as well. The Hill’s Mike Lillis breaks down for Insider where else the GOP’s redistricting plan backfired.

You’re the lame ducks now — take the hard votes while you can , Jay Rogers writes in The Hill.

Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton greets supporters during an election night event, Nov. 3, 2026, in Overland Park, Kansas. (Charlie Riedel, Associated Press)

And finally … It’s Thursday, which means it’s time for the weekly news quiz!

Democrats put up a historic performance in this year’s midterms, having won at least 54 Senate seats and eyeing 250 seats or more in the House. This week’s quiz will look back at some of the memorable midterm waves for both parties.

articles.title: On the Ballot: Meet the history-making winners of the 2026 elections
articles.summary: Democrats dominated and won back control of both the House and Senate in the blue wave of their dreams with stunning flips in red Texas, Kansas, Iowa and beyond. It was the most expensive midterm cycle on record and shattered midterm turnout benchmarks in key states. In many races, Democrats notched their first win in eons: James…
articles.body:
Democrats dominated and won back control of both the House and Senate in the blue wave of their dreams with stunning flips in red Texas, Kansas, Iowa and beyond.

It was the most expensive midterm cycle on record and shattered midterm turnout benchmarks in key states. In many races, Democrats notched their first win in eons: James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won the Senate and governorship in Texas after decades of blue losses, and Kansas flipped in the Senate race for the first time in almost a century.

But the midterm elections were historic for another reason: voters elected barrier-breaking candidates to Congress and other top positions.

Here are a few of the standout firsts of the 2026 elections:

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated President Trump -backed Mike Rogers in Michigan’s marquee Senate race, becoming the first Muslim American elected to the Senate.

Born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrant parents, El-Sayed weathered attacks against his background from Republicans who sought to question his loyalty to the U.S. Rogers raised alleged links between the Democrat and the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group that El-Sayed has disavowed . Trump labeled the Democrat as a “violent terrorist” and called him by his middle name, “Mohamed.”

Four Muslim Americans serve in the House, according to data from the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), but El-Sayed will be sworn in as the first in the Senate.

Several Native American men have served in the upper chamber, including current Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin , but Democrat Peggy Flanagan ’s Tuesday victory for Minnesota Senate makes her the first Native American woman to join the ranks.

A citizen of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, she’d already made her mark as the first Native American woman elected to lead any national political party committee in 2023, chairing the Democratic Lieutenant Governors Association.

Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D) sailed through the election for Rep. Diana DeGette’s (D-Colo.) House seat in Colorado after defeating the longtime incumbent in the primary.

Kiros, a 29-year-old democratic socialist who was not even born when DeGette started serving in Washington, is on track to be sworn in as the first Gen-Z woman in Congress .

Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.) became the first male member of Generation Z in the House when he was elected at age 25 in 2022.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso (R) of Wisconsin’s 7 th District, left open by Rep. Tom Tiffany (R), will become the youngest member of the next congressional class. He’s 26 years old, and the first Gen Z Republican in Congress.

Rep. Chris Pappas (D) defeated former Sen. John Sununu (R-N.H.) in the Granite State and is on track to be the Senate’s first openly gay male senator.

Wisconsin Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D) was the first openly gay member elected to the upper chamber when she won her seat in 2012. There are more LGBTQ lawmakers in the House, with 11 members breaking the record for representation four years ago, according to Pew Research of the current Congress.

Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland made history in 2021 when she became the first Indigenous woman to hold a cabinet position in the White House. She’s charting another first after becoming the first Native American woman to be elected a governor.

The Democrat won New Mexico’s race on Tuesday alongside Lt. Gov.-elect Stephanie Garcia Richard , marking the first all-women-of-color gubernatorial ticket, according to data from the Center for American Women and Politics (CAWP).

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor’s mansion in Georgia, becoming the nation’s first Black female governor.

She beat out Republican billionaire Rick Jackson for the seat and is also set to become the first Democrat to hold the Peach State’s top office in over two decades. She’ll also be governor of the state where her great-great grandparents were once enslaved, according to family history she shared to social media.

More candidates made history in their states Democrat Amy Acton will be Ohio’s first female governor. Republican Marsha Blackburn was voted in as the first female governor in Tennessee. Democrat Xavier Becerra will be California’s first Latino governor in more than a century.

Meanwhile, Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in Florida, Democrat Aaron Ford of Nevada and Democrat David Crowley in Wisconsin are set to be the first Black governors of their respective states.

Illinois is now the first state with two women of color in the Senate at once after Democrat Juliana Stratton , the lieutenant governor who will now become the sixth Black woman to serve in the upper chamber, won her race and joins Sen. Tammy Duckworth , who was the first Thai American elected to Congress when she won in 2012.

A record three Black women will serve at the same time in the Senate for the first time, with Stratton joining Democratic Sens. Angela Alsobrooks (Md.) and Lisa Blunt Rochester (Del.).

It was a record year for women candidates, according to CAWP, with more women set to serve in Congress and in statewide elected office than ever before.

Welcome to The Hill’s On The Ballot. If you were able to get five or more consecutive hours of sleep between Wednesday and Thursday, count yourself a star. (We’re not sharing our sleep scores with you here, this is our newsletter.) We’re Julia Mueller and Caroline Vakil — reach out to us on X ( @jmthewriter + @CarolineVakil) or via email ( jmueller@thehill.com + cvakil@thehill.com.)

The turnout numbers coming in across the country spell out a historic night, with voters smashing records in some of the cycle’s most critical battlegrounds.

More than 50 million ballots were cast during early voting, outpacing the last midterms in states with major Senate fights, according to analysis from the New York Times, including Texas, North Carolina, Michigan and Ohio.

Texans broke their state’s early-voting record with 7.7 million ballots cast, compared to 5.5 million in 2022, marking the biggest turnout jump. Another 2.8 million people voted early in each of North Carolina and Georgia, up from 2.2 million and 2.5 million in 2022, respectively.

In a hint of what was to come for Democrats, early and mail votes were bluer this year than they were in 2024, according to a DDHQ breakdown.

In North Carolina, early ballots broke for Republicans by one point in 2024, but for Democrats by 12 points this year, a 13-point swing as Democrat Roy Cooper won the state. Early votes in Kansas broke for Republicans by 18 points in 2024 but just one point this year, a 17-point difference as Democrat Adam Hamilton flipped the red stronghold.

Election Day ballots added fuel to the blue wave and broke more records in key states.

Voters in South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews pulled off a Senate race upset, hit the state’s highest levels of participation in decades for both the total ballots cast and the percentage of registered voters participating.

Minnesota, Maine and Michigan also broke records for ballots cast in a non-presidential year. Missouri also appeared headed toward a milestone as votes rolled in.

Democrats from New Hampshire to Wisconsin are on track to make massive inroads in state legislatures across the country, as the party’s runs up wins up and down the ballot. Here’s more from Caroline.

The massive Democratic victories seen across the country on Tuesday are standing to shake up the 2028 presidential landscape as Republicans reckon with their post-Trump future. The Hill’s Julia Manchester and Mallory Wilson report.

Democrats exceeded even their own expectations in a big night Tuesday to coast to comfortable majorities in both the House and Senate, The Hill’s Jared Gans reports.

As the midterm cycle draws to a close and we look to 2028, here’s a roundup of what fueled candidates, strategists and experts on the campaign trail.

South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D) was reading “Winn Dixie” by Kate DiCamillo with her daughter — while rival outgoing Sen. Darline Graham had just read “Tuesdays with Morrie” by Mitch Abom. Independent Dan Osborn , who fell short against Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) in Nebraska, had just finished “A People’s History of the United States” by Howard Zinn.

Melat Kiros , the Democrat replacing incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette (D) in Colorado’s 1st District, favored iced matcha. Republican Billionaire Rick Jackson , who lost his bid for Georgia governor, was getting energy from a “quad latte” from Starbucks. Democratic Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree in Maine, was fueling up with “straight-up coffee.”

Kyle Kondik , the managing editor at Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics, said it was “important for my health” to have cheese on hand as he analyzed this year’s elections. Rep. Kevin Kiley (Calif.), a former Republican who lost his bid for a third term as an independent, had popcorn on deck.

What album or podcast do you have on repeat?

Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan was listening to politics and policy podcasts, including “Ones and Tooze” and “The Rest is Politics.” His across-the-aisle competitor, Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers , on the other hand, was “more of a radio guy,” tuning into WJR and true crime on Dateline or Red Eye Radio. Democrat David Hogg, who leads the Leaders We Deserve PAC, was playing Pink Pantheress’s “Fancy That.”

What TV show are you watching right now?

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg was “very excited” for the next season of Apple TV’s “Slow Horses.” Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), Florida’s next governor, was about to start season three of Apple TV’s “Silo.” Jaime Harrison, a former chair of the Democratic National Committee, was tuned into “Ghosts” on CBS.

Democrats routed Republicans in the House and clawed back the Senate majority. But that’s not all: Democrats also dominated statewide races that could be key to shaping the national political landscape through the end of Trump’s second term and beyond.

Five governor’s mansions are projected to flip blue with two more on the horizon as of late Wednesday , which could deprive Republicans of any gubernatorial gains this cycle.

The Democratic momentum also reverberated through attorneys general races, with a stunning upset in Texas.

Democrat Nathan Johnson emerged the victor over Trump-backed Republican Mayes Middleton, flipping a seat that current Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton held for three terms before opting for an unsuccessful Senate bid this year instead of seeking a fourth term.

The flip is poised to be a dramatic shift for the Lone Star State office, which aggressively pursued legal action against the Obama and Biden administrations and, under Paxton, was criticized as too politicized.

In Georgia, Democrat Tanya Miller flipped the AG’s office and became the first woman to serve in the role in Peach State history. And in Iowa, Democrat Nate Willems took the office from Republican incumbent Brenna Bird.

Democratic attorneys general have been a key force in the party’s resistance to the Trump administration, and this year’s AG upsets, paired with Democratic wins up and down ballot, could reshape politics and policy in traditionally red states.

The blue wave also crashed into secretary of state races, with a handful of wins that make Democrats the top election officials in important 2028 battlegrounds.

In Georgia, Democrat Penny Reynolds will take over from Republican SOS Brad Raffenspberger, who drew Trump’s ire for resisting his calls to overturn the Peach State’s 2020 results. In Ohio, Democrat Allison Russo will succeed outgoing Republican SOS Frank LaRose.

Democrats also broke through GOP trifectas in state Legislatures across the country, winning the majorities in at least 10 state chambers, including the long-red Texas House – all signs that the party’s sought-after blue wave turned out to be a blue tsunami.

articles.title: The blue wave that the DNC built: Behind the scenes of Democrats’ historic election sweep
articles.summary: When Ken Martin became chairman of the Democratic National Committee in February 2025, he said the party must “organize everywhere and compete everywhere so we can win anywhere.” The early returns on that bet came in long before Tuesday.
articles.body:
On Nov. 4, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) stood at a podium in Tallahassee and called Tuesday’s results “an extinction-level event for Republicans across the country.”

He wasn’t exaggerating. By early estimates , Democrats are on track to win the national House vote by 13 to 14 points, the largest margin for either party since 1974. Two years ago, Democrats lost that same vote by 2.6 points. That is a swing of more than 15 points in a single cycle.

To understand how, look at where Democrats won.

Democrats flipped seven Senate seats on Tuesday and lost none. They won in Texas, Ohio. Iowa. Kansas. South Carolina. North Carolina. Maine. In the House, Democrats have flipped at least 40 seats . Democrats won governorships in Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Georgia. In Iowa alone, Democrats flipped three House seats . Democrats also flipped control of 10 statehouses and gained 585 statehouse seats.

Most of yesterday’s map runs through states President Trump carried. For years, the Democratic Party treated many of those states as lost causes. None of them flipped because of what happened on Election Day, or even the few weeks before. The groundwork for yesterday’s victories began 21 months ago.

When Ken Martin became chairman of the Democratic National Committee in February 2025, he made a bet. He said that the DNC must “ organize everywhere and compete everywhere so we can win anywhere .” He had run that play before — as chair of the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, he went 25-0 in statewide races .

The early returns on that bet came in long before Tuesday. Under Martin, Democrats flipped 31 state legislative seats from red to blue since Trump took office, and lost none. Democrats won or overperformed in roughly 90 percent of the races the DNC tracked.

25-0 in Minnesota. 31-0 in statehouse flips. 7-0 in the Senate. 40 seats flipped in the House.

That record was built, one efficient dollar at a time. Here’s what the DNC did.

First, it provided money for every state party, every month. Through its State Partnership Program , more informally known as the 57 State Strategy, the DNC sent $17,500 a month to every state and territorial party, plus another $5,000 a month to Republican-controlled states . In total, the Democrats’ national party committees moved $38.9 million into state parties this cycle through September.

That steady money raised both the floor and the ceiling of what was possible on Tuesday. When voters turned on the Trump administration, Democrats already had people on the ground to meet them. In Maine, the program added staff to build a full-time professional operation. And last night, Maine finally retired Sen. Susan Collins (R).

Second, Democrats listened to the voters. Through its Local Listeners program , the DNC called 450,000 Democrats who voted in 2020 and stayed home in 2024, and held 10,000 real conversations with them in 61 battleground districts. These were difficult conversations to have, but we needed to know why we lost these voters so we could learn and improve.

On Tuesday, those voters — and many more like them — came back. Latino support for Democrats rose from 55 percent in 2024 to 65 percent this year. Independents, who split roughly evenly two years ago, broke for Democrats by about 17 points.

Third, the DNC invested in people. The national party trained 25,000 organizers and nearly 350 campaign staffers in regional bootcamps across all 50 states. It paid more than 120 fellows to register voters , adding more than 7,200 in Arizona alone, and funded senior staff in the battleground states of Arizona, Nevada and Pennsylvania.

Finally, the DNC worked to protect the vote. Last year, five states had voter protection programs ; today, 37 do. The DNC’s legal team also won injunctions against both of Trump’s executive orders on elections.

None of this is glamorous work. But thanks to Martin’s DNC, all of it was in place before the first ad aired.

Elon Musk spent roughly $446 million to elect Republicans, including $158 million that flowed through a Senate super PAC to back Ken Paxton in Texas. Outside groups spent more than $316 million on Paxton alone. He still lost to James Talarico by about 12 points .

Since Labor Day, Republican groups poured more than $740 million into congressional races. Democrats swept on Tuesday anyway.

That was the plan a lot of D.C. consultants wanted the DNC to follow: bank the cash, spend it on television in the fall, pack up the morning after. But Martin refused to play the same old game.

Democrats know the late-money model well, because we’ve run it ourselves. I’ve sat in those rooms. I watched us do it. An independent autopsy of the 2024 cycle found that Democrats spent nearly $9 billion and left no permanent infrastructure behind. Republicans just learned the same lesson at Musk’s expense.

The skeptics will say this was a wave, and that any DNC chair would have ridden it. But waves don’t build boats. All you need to do is look at Texas.

Texas has been Democrats’ white whale for a generation. No Democrat had won statewide there in 32 years . In 2018, Beto O’Rourke came within 3 points of a Senate flip, and Democrats still won nothing statewide.

But this time, the boat was already built. Not only did Talarico win his Senate seat, but Gina Hinojosa (D) unseated Gov. Greg Abbott (R). And with nearly every vote counted, Democrats appear to have swept Texas’s statewide offices , from lieutenant governor to railroad commissioner.

If Democrats can compete for Texas’s 40 electoral votes, the 2028 map no longer looks like any map we have drawn before.

Martin and the Democratic Party built it. Now they need to keep it.

Michael Kapp is a member of the Democratic National Committee and its Rules and Bylaws Committee.
