articles.title: DeSantis: ‘No question’ midterms a ‘rebuke’ of Trump, Congress
articles.summary: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) cast blame on Congress and President Trump after Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections. “This midterm, no question, was a rebuke of the president and the Congress by Democrats, independents and some Republicans that crossed over,” he told Fox News’s Laura Ingraham. “But a lot of our voters…
articles.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) cast blame on Congress and President Trump after Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections.

“This midterm, no question, was a rebuke of the president and the Congress by Democrats, independents and some Republicans that crossed over,” he told Fox News’s Laura Ingraham.

“But a lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate,” the governor continued. “That’s just a fact. They were promised big things, and they didn’t deliver it.”

Exit polling from Tuesday indicated that economic issues were the central motivating factor for many voters in this election, with 75 percent of voters in a CBS News poll saying the condition of the U.S. economy was “not good.”

An analysis by The New York Times , looking at nationwide exit surveys, found that voters from every demographic moved toward favoring Democratic candidates in this election from 2024.

The Democratic Party secured notable victories in red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina and flipped control of both chambers of Congress, results that have been labeled a “ blue tsunami .”

In DeSantis’s Florida, Democrats gained ground in state races and defeated GOP candidates for House seats, although Republicans maintained control of other major statewide offices.

The GOP issued their own analysis of what went wrong in Tuesday’s election. Texas Sens. John Cornyn (R) and Ted Cruz (R) responded to the historic defeats of Republican candidates in their state’s Senate and gubernatorial races on Wednesday.

In an op-ed published in The Wall Street Journal, titled “ Republicans Forgot How to Win Elections ,” Cornyn said the GOP failed on four fronts in the midterms: broad voter appeal, candidate likeability, ability to deliver on promises and integrity.

“This week’s beat-down wasn’t only foreseeable, it was foreseen,” the Republican, who lost his reelection primary bid to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, added.

Cruz warned that Texans would be “hurt” after Democratic state Reps. James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won the state’s Senate and gubernatorial races, respectively.

“Texas is blue. That is a hard sentence to utter,” the senator wrote on social media . “But Texas, today at least, is blue.”

He continued, “As we sit here today, I am the only statewide elected Republican who remains in Texas. That’s not something I ever thought I would say.”

articles.title: El-Sayed: Michigan rejected ‘hateful, spiteful campaign’

Mike Rogers (R), in the state’s Senate race. “Michigan proved just how big we are,” El-Sayed told The Associated Press, after he was projected the winner. “Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say…
articles.body:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) on Wednesday said Michigan “rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign” run by his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R), in the state’s Senate race .

“Michigan proved just how big we are,” El-Sayed told The Associated Press , after he was projected the winner.

“Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face,” he continued. “Michiganders rejected that. Every single county, every single one, pushed against that.”

The Democrat, who is set to become the first Muslim senator , faced attacks on his faith and family background on the campaign trail from Rogers, President Trump and Vice President Vance.

The GOP nominee claimed the progressive candidate had “ pledged his support ” to the Muslim Brotherhood, which the Trump administration designated as a terrorist group last year.

El-Sayed repeatedly pushed back on these accusations, saying he was “proud to be an American” when asked about them during a fiery debate .

“I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray,” he continued. “And the question that you would ask that, I think, is actually really quite shameful.”

The incoming senator told the AP on Wednesday afternoon he had still not spoken to Rogers after the Republican issued a concession statement earlier in the day.

In the statement, Rogers extended his gratitude to the Michiganders who supported his campaign and issued a warning.

“Michigan — we have a state to save, now more than ever,” he said. “Our work continues, and I remain hopeful that Michigan’s best days are ahead.”

El-Sayed defeated the Republican candidate by around 7 percentage points, according to results from Decision Desk HQ on Wednesday afternoon.

The Michigan Democrat told the newswire that he took “a moment of reflection” on his historic victory Wednesday morning, thinking about what it would mean for his two young daughters.

“Now, this is something they read about in the history books,” he added.

articles.title: Hey, fellow Republicans. Tired of winning yet?
articles.summary: The 2026 Republican bloodbath rests totally on President Trump.
articles.body:
President Trump has broken his promise to Republicans that we were going to win so much we would get tired of winning.

He has spent the entirety of his second term paying attention only to his base, which is not even close to a majority of the electorate. Amazingly, Trump has managed to tarnish the MAGA brand so much that now it has a higher unfavorable rating than the Democratic Socialists of America.

Yet Trump led the Republican messaging in the midterms, with his 37 percent approval rating, pleading with voters to pretend he was on the ballot. They did, and the result was a good old-fashioned whooping on Republicans up and down the ballot.

This was pure political malpractice driven by Trump himself. Contrary to MAGA doctrine, being president does not make you a political genius.

Here is what the president said on Oct. 24 in Georgia: “The United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars. I don’t give a damn, I’m going to say it — we’re making a freaking fortune.”

He conveniently left out that those billions of dollars come out of the pockets of hardworking American families. Most of them vote.

Republicans lost at least 24 House seats (probably many more) and seven Senate seats , with Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi still undecided.

Trump pushed Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) out of his reelection campaign. Republicans lost the seat . Trump pushed Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) out of her reelection campaign. Republicans lost the seat . Likewise, Trump’s attacks pushed popular Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) into retirement . Republicans lost the seat .

In October, Trump attacked Florida Republican Rep. Maria Salazar (R-Fla.) on her immigration position. It may have helped Salazar, who stood up to Trump’s very unpopular Immigration and Customs Enforcement immigration raids, save her seat by a whisker .

Most egregious of all, in Texas, Trump endorsed Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R). Paxton had a record of multiple legal and ethical problems . Cornyn had a record of overwhelming support for Trump. Republicans spent millions of dollars trying to save Paxton. That is money that could have been spent to win Ohio or Iowa. Instead, Republicans lost even the Texas seat .

In South Carolina, Trump pushed Darline Graham, sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, into running following her appointment to finish out her brother’s term. He did so because the alternative was Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) who had incurred Trump’s wrath by supporting his former governor, Nikki Haley, in the 2024 presidential primaries. Republicans lost the seat .

The 2026 Republican bloodbath rests totally on President Trump.

Fifteen months ago, I wrote on these pages that the MAGA agenda was pushing Trump out of the mainstream. As the his second term unfolded, it became obvious that his preoccupation with issues most voters did not care about was becoming a big problem.

As American families became more and more concerned about the rising costs of groceries, the president told them those price increases were “ peanuts ” and a Democratic “ hoax .” The 2026 midterm election cried out to be localized by Republican candidates. The president refused to let this happen. In the “me” presidency, everything must be about him.

Bad political decisions by the president have ended the careers of promising up and coming Republicans. This election’s bad effects on Republicans are not over. While the media focused on the congressional outcomes, hundreds of state legislative races around the country were still decided. Republican candidates in those state legislative races ran against the same undertow that the Trump administration produced nationally.

Going forward, the state and local results will be a big problem. The Republican bench has been decimated. In 2028, freshman Democrats in Congress will face an easier reelection because their toughest Republican opponent will have lost his or her down-ballot reelection in 2026.

So, if you are a somewhat young conservative who believes in limited government, the Constitution, government efficiency and strong loyalty to a set of governing principles rather than to an individual, then there is a city or county council seat or a state legislative seat which beckons to you.

Kevin Igoe is the former deputy chief of staff of the Republican National Committee and former executive director of the Maryland Republican Party. He served as chief of staff of the Maryland Department of Budget and Management and was a Reagan White House appointee.

articles.title: Hegseth's leadership questioned by GOP military veteran as Democrats talk impeachment
articles.summary: Rep. Don Bacon alleges Pete Hegseth lacks a "moral compass" and says the secretary "doesn't have a lot of friends on the Hill" today.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., told Fox News Digital that the Department of War should not be led by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, criticizing his leadership and questioning his judgment. Bacon, who questioned Hegseth's "moral compass," made his remarks after Democrats reclaimed control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, raising the possibility of impeachment proceedings against members of President Donald Trump's Cabinet in the 120th Congress. "I don't think he was a good choice to begin with," Bacon told Fox News Digital. "I wouldn't have voted to confirm him." Bacon, a 30-year Air Force veteran, argued that Hegseth's personal conduct would have resulted in disciplinary action for other members of the military. GOP SEN THOM TILLIS URGES TRUMP TO REPLACE PETE HEGSETH, BLASTS PENTAGON LEADERSHIP "Anybody that got caught having affairs would've gotten fired," Bacon said before pointing to the controversy surrounding the administration's use of the Signal messaging app to discuss sensitive military operations. HEGSETH FIRES TOP PENTAGON STRATEGIST ACCUSED OF LEAKING CLASSIFIED IRAN, UKRAINE WAR INFORMATION "He didn't take any responsibility for it, though it was his fault. And things like that bother folks who've served a lifetime in the military, have a moral compass and take responsibility," Bacon continued. GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH Bacon also suggested that Hegseth lacks substantial support among lawmakers on Capitol Hill, where a Democratic-controlled House could pursue impeachment proceedings against the war secretary. Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell responded to Bacon's remarks in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying Hegseth "will not back down" or "be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists." Without mentioning Bacon by name, Parnell added that Hegseth "will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America" on behalf of President Donald Trump, "despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump’s term in office." Toward the end of the 119th Congress, a group of Democrats backed legislation introduced by Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., seeking to impeach Hegseth. ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH "Hegseth doesn't have a lot of friends on the Hill," Bacon said while discussing whether Trump should replace the war secretary before possible impeachment proceedings. "I do think we could have more qualified leaders." Trump told reporters Wednesday that he intends to keep Hegseth in his Cabinet, despite speculation about the war secretary's future. DEMOCRAT SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN The president's comments came after other Cabinet departures during his second term, including former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Attorney General Pam Bondi, who were asked to resign. During his interview with Fox News Digital, Bacon addressed the future of the Republican Party following its midterm defeat, arguing that the GOP must distance itself from Trump to regain congressional majorities, win governorships and remain competitive in the 2028 presidential election. Bacon did not dismiss the idea of running for president himself when asked by Fox News Digital, and has previously said in podcast interviews that he would "love" to. MIKE JOHNSON'S NO 2 LAUNCHES GOP TAKEOVER BID AS HOUSE FALLS TO DEMOCRATS "I do think we should have a big debate in our party," Bacon said, leaving open the possibility of playing a role in the party's future leadership. "I'd like to fight for the soul of our party. And I want to be a part of that discussion, that debate." "If somebody steps up and wants to take on the little more of the Reagan mantle and the sort of things I think need to get done to the country," the retired one-star Air Force general continued. "I'm glad to support them. But somebody's got to be speaking out against illegal immigration, cost of healthcare, and national security policy, and they got to be able, we'll work across the aisle to get things done. You can't solve this from all your Democrats only." Bacon argued that Republicans should return to the principles championed by former President Ronald Reagan, including "the basic principles of economic freedom, free markets and free trade, peace through strength, stand up to the bully, which in this case, is Russia." He also emphasized the importance of "federalism and the pro-life movement" as priorities for the party moving forward. The Nebraska Republican criticized Trump's approach to traditional U.S. allies, arguing that the administration has been "very bad towards our allies," including Canada and Greenland, amid disputes over tariffs and the president's threats involving Greenland. Bacon suggested that Trump's foreign policy decisions and military involvement overseas contributed to Republican losses in down-ballot races across the country. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "They only got beat because they had an R next to their name," Bacon said, accusing congressional Republicans of having "rubber-stamped" the president's agenda since he returned to the White House for a second term.

articles.title: Republican AGs stand ready as 'last line of defense' against leftist policies after dismal midterms for party
articles.summary: Republican Attorneys General Association memo reveals GOP AG candidates ran 4.62 points ahead of Senate hopefuls across key midterm election states.
articles.body: Republican attorney general candidates outperformed other midterm GOP hopefuls in several key races, according to a post-election analysis from the Republican Attorneys General Association, which urged colleagues to view their role as the "front line" against leftist policies following results that were likened to a "category-five political hurricane." "America needs Republican Attorneys General now more than ever," RAGA Executive Director Adam Piper wrote in a late-night memo to colleagues shared with Fox News Digital. "With an emboldened Democrat Congress, Republican AGs are both America’s front line and is the last line of defense when it comes to their left-wing wish list – such as court packing, the Green New Deal, Medicare for All, Second Amendment restrictions, and abolishing ICE." Piper, who has worked in Virginia and on the staff of South Carolina Gov.-elect Alan Wilson, noted midterm election results showed Republican attorneys general candidates holding up slightly better on ballots despite a difficult Tuesday night for the party. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI "Last night was the worst election night for the Republican Party in 50 years," Piper's memo began, acknowledging a difficult midterm "environment" that was ultimately made worse. "Last night, voters, regardless of party, preferred Democrat candidates by a mean of D +13.8 compared to D +7.9 in 2006 and D +8.4 in 2018. "Today, we are dealing with the aftermath of a category-five political hurricane. It will take years to fully rebuild." As Republicans are picking up the pieces and evaluating the map overcome with blue, even along wide swaths of Texas' southern border, the party is looking to the slight holds in Florida and any other silver linings. Attorneys general might have something in the way of a pep talk for the party from Piper's memo. GOP AG candidates ran an average of 4.62 percentage points ahead of GOP Senate candidates in comparable states and 2.12 points ahead of Republican gubernatorial candidates, according to the returns as of the late Wednesday night memo. Republican AG candidates posted better margins than GOP Senate candidates in nine of 10 comparable states and outperformed Republican gubernatorial candidates in nine of 13 states, Piper wrote. STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE Still, Piper made clear that "there are no moral victories." Republicans did lose five AG seats to Democrats in these midterms, compared to a projected net loss of 51 in the House and a potential net loss of nine Senate seats. Iowa, Ohio and Colorado were among the widest outperformers. The Republican attorney general candidates in those states ran 9.3, 7.3 and 10.3 points ahead of their party’s gubernatorial candidates, respectively. In Colorado, the GOP attorney general candidate also outpaced the Republican Senate candidate by 7.7 points. FLORIDA'S DESANTIS DESCRIBES GOP MIDTERMS WIPEOUT AS 'CLOSE TO AN EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' FOR REPUBLICANS In Florida, now the largest red state with the handing over of Texas to the Democratic Party, Republican Attorney General James Uthmeier won by 1.8 percentage points, outperforming Gov.-elect Byron Donalds, who won by 1.3 points. Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers won re-election by 12.6 points, compared with a 6.7-point win for Republican Senate candidate Pete Ricketts and an 8.4-point victory for Republican Gov. Jim Pillen. RAGA spent more than $40 million on these midterms, nearly twice its spending in 2022, and was on track to raise more than $50 million, according to Piper. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "No amount of outperformance can make up for the historical Republican losses," his memo concluded. "RAGA will start to candidate recruit for 2027 and 2028 now and has set the expectation that we will continue to overperform, no matter the environment."

articles.title: I lost my period for 2 decades — I wish I had known what I know now
articles.summary: A new initiative on women’s health could have saved me years of pain related to infertility. I’m hoping it will help others.
articles.body:
For more than 20 years — during the peak of my childbearing years — I did not have my period.

My menstrual cycle had stopped during my college soccer career, and countless doctors and healthcare professionals told me this was “normal” for female athletes. At the time I believed them — I assumed that once I stopped playing soccer and entered nursing school, my cycle would return.

It didn’t. And the ramifications of not menstruating would significantly impact my emotional and physical well-being for the next two decades.

Later, as I learned about cooperative women’s healthcare through FACTS About Fertility, I discovered that all of those reassurances were wrong. The ovulatory-menstrual cycle is a vital sign of health. And, after working with a new family physician and other professionals who accurately understand the female cycle’s essential role in health and fertility, I got my period again. My cycles are now normal.

Medical professionals trained in identifying and addressing root causes see the lack of a period for what it is: a signal. And they treat it accordingly. This is the exact outcome the Department of Health and Human Services desires with recent grants for an infertility training center , as well as a presidential executive order concerning women’s health that was signed just last month in the Rose Garden.

With the order, Advancing Women’s Health to Improve Outcomes in All Phases of Life, a new White House Task Force on Women’s Health will be convened, and a Women’s Health Division will be created at the National Institutes of Health. As an advanced practice registered nurse, I know that the needs have never been greater for the nearly 174 million women who make up our country’s population. Approximately 20 percent of women report at least one reproductive health condition, and 1 in 6 adults worldwide experiences infertility in their lifetime.

Thirteen years ago, with a diagnosis of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, I was told that I would never be able to conceive naturally because I wasn’t ovulating. This was devastating for my husband and me. They said that there was no treatment, but that I shouldn’t worry because I was “so fit and healthy.” I also was told that changing my diet and exercise regimen would not affect my hormones or bring back my cycle.

I was fit, but I was not healthy. When you don’t ovulate, the underlying condition must be addressed. Too often, the only option given women in my circumstance is to undergo rounds of in vitro fertilization, which I did. But IVF did not treat the root causes of my reproductive and hormonal health issues.

IVF brings its own physical risks as well as emotional and financial stressors that can be devastating. My husband and I were not immune, and on many levels, it was soul crushing. Today, I know there is another way.

In the spring of 2024, I was introduced to the concepts of the female cycle as a vital sign, fertility awareness-based methods and body literacy through organizations like FACTS — the Fertility Appreciation Collaborative to Teach the Science — and FEMM — Fertility Education and Medical Management . With this information, I began to wonder why no medical professional ever explained to me how destructive anovulation and lack of a period was to my bones, heart and hormones. I also began to question why I had been told that IVF was the only solution to my infertility.

I wish I could tell my 20-year-old self about the things I’ve learned. It is not normal for one’s period to stop, and being fit doesn’t always mean healthy. Low blood pressure and heart rate can be signs of insufficient energy intake. Additionally, exercise and nutrition changes can tremendously impact your menstrual cycle, all of your hormones and your overall health. And IVF is not the only option for women with hypothalamic amenorrhea who wish to become pregnant.

I do not share my personal story for sympathy or to imply that I would change my past, because I wouldn’t change my journey with my five healthy, incredible children for anything in this world.

I share my story, however, to highlight the imperative need for a better healthcare system for women — a system that highlights the importance of educating women about their bodies and menstrual cycles while simultaneously ensuring that healthcare professionals treat all reproductive health concerns from a root-cause approach. And I hope some of these recent grants and initiatives will help secure that for women like me.

Shannon Leach is a mother of five and lives with her husband and children in Everett, Wash. She has been an advanced registered nurse practitioner since 2011 and works for 3W Medical for Women in Seattle and Cascade Women’s Health .

articles.title: At 26, Sean Duffy's son-in-law is headed to Congress as its youngest member
articles.summary: Michael Alfonso, 26, won Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District with Trump's endorsement and plans to push affordability and reigniting the American dream.
articles.body: Michael Alfonso is set to become the youngest member of Congress at 26 years old after winning a key Wisconsin House seat. Alfonso, a Republican, will head to Washington this January after running a campaign focused on delivering on affordability and restoring the American Dream, two priorities he emphasized throughout his campaign. articles.title: Could a rogue clerk bollix House control on Jan. 3? It’s not quite that simple.
articles.summary: Former House Rules Committee chief of staff Don Wolfensberger analyzed a historical precedent where a House clerk could potentially obstruct the seating of members-elect to manipulate congressional control.
articles.body:
In a recent op-ed , President Bill Clinton’s former Treasury Secretary, Robert E. Rubin, startled me with bizarre twist on potential electoral manipulation. Like others before him , Rubin boldly suggests that President Trump and his allies could also exploit “a procedural loophole involving the Clerk of the House that could enable them to refuse to seat duly elected Democratic members when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3.”

Rubin does not elaborate on what that procedural loophole is, nor did he respond to several requests I made by e-mail asking him to explain. After discussing this with knowledgeable experts, I concluded he was probably referring to the fact that the clerk for a new Congress, by long-standing custom, is the carryover clerk from the previous Congress. Today that clerk is Kevin McCumber, elected by the Republican majority in 2023. By all accounts, McCumber is highly thought of on both sides of the aisle.

That leads to speculation that House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) may oust him before noon on Jan. 3 when the new Congress convenes and replace him with a new clerk more amenable to cooking the election-count books.

How could the clerk be able to omit from his rollcall of members-elect certain individuals or states, thus disenfranchising them and thereby swinging majority control of the House back to the Republicans? Keep in mind that an election can be contested by a losing candidate or by protest from another member-elect. However, at least in recent times that does not entitle the clerk to refuse to recognize the certificate of election presented by a state’s designated top election official (e.g., the governor or secretary of state). Those contests are investigated by the House Administration Committee , but in the meantime the challenged members are provisionally sworn and seated.

It wasn’t until I explored the historical record that I realized it has not always been so. In the 19th century, the office of clerk was highly partisan, and there were several instances in which clerks simply refused to call the names of certain members thereby blocking their being sworn and seated.

In 1863, House clerk Amerson Etheridge excluded 16 members-elect from his call of the roll , including from five pro-Union states, while including three members from Louisiana. That effort failed, and a new clerk, Edward McPherson, was then elected. However, two years later, in 1865, during reconstruction, McPherson omitted the names of members-elect from the states of Tennessee, Virginia and Louisiana, thereby allowing the Radical Republicans to take control of the House, elect their Speaker, Thaddeus Stevens, and override many vetoes by President Andrew Johnson.

In 1839, in a dispute over the clerk refusing to include the five New Jersey members-elect on the roll , there was considerable debate over the legitimacy of a non-elected clerk in a new Congress unilaterally disqualifying certain members-elect. In that instance, a motion was offered to let the House determine whether to seat the five. When the clerk refused to recognize the motion, one member offered a motion to elect the oldest member of the House to be chairman of the body. When he refused the offer, another motion was offered to elect Rep. John Quincy Adams as chairman of the House until a Speaker was elected. That motion was adopted.

The prospect of a clerk assuming the powers once exercised by the office some two centuries ago boggles the mind. But it is reminiscent of the electoral vote count on Jan. 6, 2021, when Trump attempted to pressure Vice President Mike Pence, presiding over the joint session, to invalidate the presidential election results. Pence refused, explaining that he could not do it under the Constitution because his role was strictly administrative in nature, with no discretion to disallow the votes of any state.

When it was rumored that the Speaker might fire the current House clerk and install a new one just before the new Congress convenes, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), ranking member on the House Intelligence Committee, exclaimed that is a “ break the glass scenario for us .”

Fortunately, the precedents are clear that in the absence of a clerk, the House must proceed immediately to the election of a new one. The Speaker may remove a clerk, but he may not appoint a new one. An interim appointment or elevation of the deputy clerk, will not suffice. The House is the ultimate arbiter of any election contests, just as it is over the election of its Speaker, its clerk, and other officers.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran culminating as chief of staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of, “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial” (2000), and, “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays” (2018).

articles.title: Trump defends Hegseth but acknowledges easier path to replacing him before new Congress
articles.summary: President Trump said Thursday morning he intends to keep Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in his current role but acknowledged it would be easier to confirm someone new to lead the Pentagon before Democrats take control of Congress next year. The president told ABC News’s Jonathan Karl that he has “every intention” of keeping Hegseth in…
articles.body:
President Trump said Thursday morning he intends to keep Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in his current role but acknowledged it would be easier to confirm someone new to lead the Pentagon before Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The president told ABC News’s Jonathan Karl that he has “every intention” of keeping Hegseth in the Cabinet , following reporting Wednesday that he was weighing whether the Defense chief should stay in the post after the midterm elections.

Trump said he’s received calls from people who are concerned about Hegseth but noted he didn’t “understand why.”

On Wednesday, he suggested Hegseth would be “ very popular ” if he was elected to replace Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) in Congress; Blackburn opted to run for Tennessee governor instead of reelection. Trump also said the Defense secretary was “doing a very good job.”

Hegseth previously expressed interest in Blackburn’s seat, two sources familiar with the matter told The Hill at the end of October. A third person said the Pentagon leader is campaigning behind the scenes for the role, while another said his interest was an open secret.

Pentagon spokesperson Kingsley Wilson denied the reports at the time as “beltway gossip by anonymous sources.”

The flip of control of Congress in favor of Democrats in Tuesday’s midterms sets new timeline pressures for the president and his administration to confirm a new Defense secretary if Hegseth were to depart the role.

Democrats will have a majority in the Senate , where Trump’s Cabinet nominees need a simple majority for confirmation. Under the chamber’s current 53-47 Republican majority, the president can afford to lose up to three GOP lawmakers.

This will not be the case in the new term, where Democrats have already secured 54 seats in the Senate and could possibly gain one more in Alaska.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is expected to become Speaker when Democrats take control , appeared to reference the Defense chief’s possible departure on Thursday morning.

“Why is Pete Hegseth still around?” he wrote on social media .

articles.title: Former Trump staffer calls for Wiles to resign over midterm wipeout
articles.summary: Caroline Sunshine, a former staffer to President Trump, on Wednesday called for White House chief of staff Susie Wiles to resign over the massive losses Republicans saw in the midterm elections. Sunshine told Fox News’s Jesse Watters on “Jesse Watters Primetime” that she was going to say “what a lot of people are saying privately.”…
articles.body:
Caroline Sunshine, a former staffer to President Trump, on Wednesday called for White House chief of staff Susie Wiles to resign over the massive losses Republicans saw in the midterm elections.

Sunshine told Fox News’s Jesse Watters on “Jesse Watters Primetime” that she was going to say “what a lot of people are saying privately.”

“Susie Wiles needs to resign,” she told Watters, causing the host to raise his eyebrows. “She needs to offer her resignation to the president before he has to ask for it. Her campaign skills have not translated into governing. Susie was behind the historic win in 2024, and she deserved credit for it and got the top job for it.”

The former Trump staffer added that Wiles was now “behind the historic loss where we lost Mississippi and have lost potentially the Senate for six years, and so that cuts both ways.”

The Mississippi Senate race remains tight between Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) and Democrat Scott Colom and has not been called by The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Colom leads Hyde-Smith with 49.04 percent of the vote to her 48.85 percent, according to DDHQ.

Sunshine said Wiles remaining in her role could cost Republicans again in 2028 and that “if she loves and respects the president and his legacy, she’ll do the right thing and step aside.”

“And a lot of this was staff failure, a lot of this was strategy and messaging failure,” Sunshine said. “It’s the chief of staff’s job to manage the staff. … Why wasn’t the staff out messaging?”

Reporting before the midterms suggested Wiles could leave the White House after the midterms. Politico reported last month that Trump had received negative feedback about Wiles from allies, though he called the story “ TOTAL FAKE NEWS ” and said Wiles “has my COMPLETE confidence.”

Trump has also publicly praised Wiles on numerous occasions. After Wiles announced she had been diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year, Trump referred to her as “an amazing person” and “an amazing fighter.” Wiles announced in September that she was cancer free .

Former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney told NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday” that he expects her to leave her post after the midterms, though not because “she’s fallen out of favor with Trump.”

“It’s just a natural sort of time to make that change,” he added.

Sarah Matthews, a former White House deputy press secretary in Trump’s first term, told MeidasTouch in October that the president was not pleased “with the way things are right now” and had floated replacement ideas to allies. She suggested that he floated the idea of replacing Wiles with the deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, an idea Matthews described as “a terrifying prospect .”

articles.summary: Mississippi's Senate race remains undecided by dozens of votes as deep-red states nearly flipped in the GOP's stunning election night bloodbath.
articles.body: Races in traditionally staunch Republican strongholds came incredibly close to flipping amid Tuesday night's landslide Democratic victory, even in states where GOP candidates enjoyed overwhelming financial advantages. Signs of something going horribly wrong for the GOP appeared late in the election cycle when Fox News rated the Senate races in South Carolina and Kansas, two states with decades-long loyalty streaks for the Republican Party, as competitive. As results poured in on election night, however, it became clear that even states that practically nobody thought would be competitive, such as Louisiana and Tennessee, were coming within a razor's edge of going blue. Mississippi, seen by most political forecasters as among the safest of GOP seats, remains undecided as of publication, with just dozens of votes separating incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and her Democratic challenger, Scott Colom. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI In Tennessee, for instance, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jerri Green spent just over $2 million, dwarfed by the nearly $13 million Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the GOP nominee, poured into the race. Outside groups burned through millions more to boost Blackburn’s candidacy. The result of outspending a Democrat by nearly 6-to-1 in one of the reddest states in the country was Blackburn defeating Green by less than three points in a state that favored Republicans by almost 30 points in 2024. Louisiana’s Senate race told a similar story. The Republican nominee, Rep. Julia Letlow, and her allies paid out approximately $9.4 million to win the seat, compared to the roughly $3.89 million Democrats spent on the race. Letlow ultimately won by just under two points in a state President Donald Trump carried by roughly 22 points in 2024, underscoring the dramatic erosion of the GOP's advantage in one of its longtime strongholds. Ron DeSantis. FIRST MUSLIM SENATOR, FIRST BLACK FEMALE GOVERNOR: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION RESULTS MAKE HISTORY Republicans outspent Democrats by roughly five-to-one in their bid for the state’s governor's mansion, ultimately winning by less than two points. Similar trends played out across the country, with multiple House and state legislative seats that Republicans won by double digits in 2024, flipping to Democratic control. articles.title: The myth of the millionaire student-athlete
articles.summary: We all know that big-revenue college sports are more about money and less about academics. Yet as the legislative clock continues, Washington must realize that managing the semi-professional sports landscape on campuses requires the ultimate safeguard: absolute transparency.
articles.body:
The march to the College Football Playoffs is underway, with numerous top 25 matchups every week keeping fans engaged. Yet behind the scenes, legal wrangling may change what happens on the field — and tarnish the very meaning of college sports and student-athletes.

The Protect College Sports Act , supported by both the Southeastern and the Big Ten conferences , is the poster child of litigious squabbling. Though it passed with bipartisan 77-22 support in the Senate, the bill is almost certain to have the clock run out when the 119th Congress ends on Jan. 3, 2027. With the results from the midterm elections and a newly shaped House taking form, student-athletes will likely receive the short end of the stick again.

The NCAA once ruled college athletics. But over the past decade, it has lost its influence over the very communities it is charged to oversee. Changes directly influenced by revenue sports like football and men’s basketball have been at the epicenter of the NCAA’s demise. Name, image and likeness rules, the ease of transferring between schools via the transfer portal and extended eligibility have all contributed to the NCAA losing its hold on college athletics for revenue sports.

Any one of these changes would have been a positive change for athletes. Together, they accelerated a disruption beyond what anyone could have imagined.

The House v. NCAA settlement last year allowed schools to pay students directly for participating, with the elite players garnering the lion’s share of the payouts. Adding in name, image and likeness revenue , facilitated by boosters , makes the environment for college revenue sports akin to minor league teams feeding the professional ranks. It also forces boosters to choose how they will allocate their gifts, either to the university or the player.

This direct compensation creep has also intensified debates over athlete employment status and collective bargaining . While the Protect College Sports Act explicitly maintains neutrality on whether athletes can unionize , transparency will inevitably clarify whether revenue-sharing functions as a form of pay.

What receives less discussion are non-revenue sports, such as the Olympics. Whether it is men’s wrestling or women’s soccer, student-athletes in these sports may get modest pay or can negotiate name, image and likeness contracts. Yet they remain students, often getting an education at no out-of-pocket cost to them, while playing a sport that they love and earning a degree that will solidify their future.

In this new environment, non-revenue sports may be squeezed by financial demands on the revenue sports, making them vulnerable to downsizing or termination. The Protect College Sports Act includes provisions to protect against such actions. The same cannot be said about all revenue sport athletes.

Some view their time on a college campus as a stepping stone to their professional career. For those good enough to be stars but who are not quite at the level to play in the professional leagues, name, name, image and likeness deals permit them to earn significant income, incentivizing them to use their full five years of eligibility. For the remaining athletes, their reward is a college degree and the opportunities it will give them upon graduation. Indeed, the Pareto Principle is at work, with a small number of athletes garnering the largest share of the money.

What all this means is that the number of college athletes who benefit is small relative to the total number of student-athletes. Even on a top-ranked football team like Ohio State , walk-ons and practice squad players fill the recently mandated 105-person roster, get to walk the sidelines during games, participate in all team activities, and earn a degree for their participation. They are the true student-athletes, though few of the team’s fans would recognize them by name or on the streets.

Instead of bemoaning how money has tarnished college sports, it is important to recognize that only a small fraction of players receive large paychecks. The infusion of revenue has created opportunities that may not have existed in the past. What is needed is more transparency around who is receiving the payouts and how much is being paid, particularly for those at the top of the heap, as stipulated by the $600 threshold in the Protect College Sports Act of 2026 .

First, it removes speculation around how money is influencing college sports. Transparency regarding such payments reveals the true cost of fielding championship teams . Second, it demonstrates how most college athletes are indeed student-athletes. Lastly, it allows competing universities to know what other schools are paying for their teams. Much like how salary caps exist for professional teams, openly sharing payments and contracts for the use of name, image and likeness creates an opportunity for leveling the playing field, as well as creating accountability for university athletic departments.

Any time money is at stake, there will be detractors fighting to maintain payment privacy. Yet for these highly paid athletes, de facto minor leaguers on a college campus, transparency works as a guardrail to protect the athletes from predatory agents and capping agent fees at 5 percent. It will also mitigate financial risks for schools.

We all know that big-revenue college sports are more about money and less about academics. Yet as the legislative clock continues, Washington must realize that managing the semi-professional sports landscape on campuses requires the ultimate safeguard: absolute transparency.

Sheldon H. Jacobson, Ph.D., is a professor of Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He applies his expertise in data-driven risk-based decision-making to evaluate and inform public policy.

articles.title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
articles.summary: Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges on allegations dating back more than 20 years.
articles.body:
LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges on allegations dating back more than 20 years.

Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand faces a “significant” prison term when he is sentenced Monday. He had been free on bail but was taken into custody.

A prosecutor said the British actor-comedian was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative “sexual predator.”

Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.

He was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London’s Metropolitan Police said the conviction was “a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them.”

“Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women,” he said. “As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement.”

The jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days.

Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

In recent years, he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

Brand said the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.

“My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations,” he said.

Brand’s lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.

Brand testified that friends and colleagues had abandoned him.

His wife, Laura, who accompanied him to court, testified as a character witness in his defense, but no one with relevant evidence was willing to give evidence on his behalf, Brand said.

articles.title: Gingrich: GOP’s massive loss takes ‘luster’ off Vance for 2028
articles.summary: Former Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.) says the massive Republican defeat in Tuesday’s elections takes “a good bit of the luster” off Vice President Vance’s expected candidacy for president in 2028 and leaves the GOP presidential primary in the next election cycle “wide open.” “The scale of the Republican defeat is so great that it makes…
articles.body:
Former Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.) says the massive Republican defeat in Tuesday’s elections takes “a good bit of the luster” off Vice President Vance’s expected candidacy for president in 2028 and leaves the GOP presidential primary in the next election cycle “wide open.”

“The scale of the Republican defeat is so great that it makes the race for the GOP presidential nomination wide open,” Gingrich posted late Wednesday on the social platform X.

“If the administration had won a big victory, Vice President JD Vance would have had an enormous argument to be the inevitable nominee,” Gingrich said.

“Now, with this go-slow strategy blowing up in Iran and his defense of Vivek Ramaswamy’s horrible, inhumane ad featuring his opponent’s mother attacking her own daughter, a good bit of luster has come off the bloom,” he argued.

Vance on Wednesday blamed the war with Iran for why Republicans got wiped out in so many gubernatorial, Senate and House races.

“The reason we lost is the war . The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a social media post .

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he argued.

“But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” Vance added.

Gingrich said the political momentum appears to be shifting to Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

“The number of people who want to draft Secretary of State Marco Rubio is staggering,” he added.

Gingrich said other potential White House candidates could benefit from the “luster” coming off Vance’s bid to become the next president.

“Ted Cruz, Tom Cotton, Ron DeSantis, Pete Hegseth, Glenn Youngkin, and a surprising number of people may decide this is their chance to take advantage of the chaos of the shocking defeat and seek to be the champion who can rescue the party and the country,” he predicted.

Cruz and Cotton are Republican senators from Texas and Arkansas, respectively. DeSantis and Youngkin are the governor and former governor of Florida and Virginia, respectively. And Hegseth is the secretary of Defense.

articles.body:
Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) on Wednesday criticized Vice President Vance’s online post in which he blamed the war in Iran for the Republican Party’s defeat in the midterms.

“Last night, the American people delivered a crystal-clear message about the mismanagement of this war, and what it has done to our pocketbooks,” Slotkin wrote in a post on the social platform X.

“Whether you supported the war or simply failed to stop it, your job is not to try and cover yourself, but to get us out of it,” she added.

In a sweeping victory, the Democrats secured control of both the House and the Senate for the next term, while flipping several GOP-held seats in battleground states like Texas, Michigan, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa.

Vance on Wednesday , in a lengthy post online , pinned the blame for the Republican Party’s midterm losses on the ongoing war in Iran.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” he wrote. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”

The ongoing Middle East conflict was a concern for voters leading up to Election Day. In a recent Gallup poll , released before the midterms, roughly 77 percent voters said the war would be an “extremely” or “very” important issue when casting their vote.

Slotkin, in her post, added, “You and President Trump got us into this war, without a clear objective and without regard for the will of the American people. It’s cost us American lives and billions of dollars of American treasure, with no end in sight.”

Trump also told The Wall Street Journal during an election night interview that the Iran war was partially to blame for the sweeping losses his party faced in the midterms.

“The decision to go to war is the most solemn responsibility that a President and Vice President have as leaders,” Slotkin wrote.

articles.title: A referendum? No, this was a full-fledged revolt
articles.summary: In a significant electoral shift, Democrats successfully channeled voter anger into aspirational messaging to win seats in deep red territories and challenge Republican gerrymandering during President Trump’s second term midterms.
articles.body:
Every consequential election produces opportunities and warnings for both parties. But this one belongs alongside the epochal wave elections of 1994 , 2006 and 2010 in its political impact and shock value.

First, Democrats may have found a way to pursue populism without the pitchfork. There’s historical irony here. In 2016 and 2024, Trump brilliantly tapped into Americans’ seething anger. Some of that anger dated to the 2008 economic financial crisis, which devastated American households and allowed the very people who ignited the crisis to profit from it. It triggered a resentment that still smolders, a sense that no one is listening and the system is rigged.

In 2016, voters wanted to send Washington a message in the form of a middle finger. Who better to deliver it than Donald Trump?

This week, Democrats ingeniously turned that anger against Trump. Listen to James Talarico in Texas, Abdul El -Sayed in Michigan, and Troy Jackson in Maine, and you heard variations on a theme: the corruption and greed of the powerful; the basic rights of ordinary Americans to see a doctor when they need one, live in safe communities and send their children to good schools.

Once again, voters sent a message to Washington, loud and clear. But Democrats found a way to deliver it without the rabid pitbull delivery of Trump. They turned their anger into aspiration without adopting his snarling rhetoric.

Second, Democrats exposed the false choice at the heart of an unnecessary feud between the left and the center. Winning doesn’t force a choice between turning out progressive voters and appealing to moderates voters. A talented candidate with a sophisticated campaign can draw both. You can thread a needle rather than poking voters in the eye.

Third, yes, even Trump can overreach. Republican gerrymandering in Florida and Texas fell short of their ambitions . In Florida, Republicans may have drawn bright red districts, but the ultimate result appeared headed toward a draw. They may retain every seat they held, but they failed to flip a single Democratic-held seat. The outcome demonstrated that a wave election can wash over gerrymandered lines.

Fourth, candidate quality matters. Trump’s ruthless abandonment of Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and his support for Sen. Darline Graham (R) in South Carolina continued a pattern of prioritizing loyalty over electability. Meanwhile, Democrats recruited candidates who reflected the priorities and sensibilities of their communities: healthcare professionals, educators, union leaders, teachers, pastors, combat veterans and even a Tejano music superstar . Voters had more to consider than a candidate’s relationship with the president.

Fifth — and I say this as both a Democrat and a Mets fan — behind every silver lining is a funereal crape. Yes, Democrats won in deep red territory, aided by anti-Trump anger, frustration over high prices and weak Republican candidates. But keeping those seats competitive in 2028 will require discipline and hard work. That means keeping new members focused on the nuts and bolts: strong constituent services, relentless visibility in their districts, and voting records that reflect the values of the people who elected them.

The good news for Democrats is that there is precedent even in this extraordinary cycle. In Trump’s first midterm, in 2018, Democrats flipped the U.S. House. Two years later, they won 13 fewer seats than they had in 2018, but they retained their majority and elected a Democratic president.

They need that same focus on winning again. Instead of debating internally and externally about a left or center agenda on Capitol Hill, they need to shift the debate to delivering back home. The candidates who won historic victories and ran competitive races in Texas, Michigan, Maine, Ohio, Mississippi, and other battlegrounds have something to teach the party. Democrats should listen.

Trump’s political success has long depended on keeping his base intensely engaged, often at the expense of appealing to voters beyond it. It is the classic case of the tail wagging the dog. This year, the dog bit back.

Steve Israel represented New York in the House of Representatives for eight terms and was chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee from 2011 to 2015.

articles.title: Carville declares DeSantis ‘Republican winner’ after midterms
articles.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville suggested Wednesday that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) was the 2026 midterms’ “Republican winner” after Democrats made sweeping gains across the country and reclaimed both chambers of Congress. Carville, political adviser Mark McKinnon and Gen Z for Change founder Aidan Kohn-Murphy were talking about the potential for a post-President Trump GOP…
articles.body:
Democratic strategist James Carville suggested Wednesday that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) was the 2026 midterms’ “Republican winner” after Democrats made sweeping gains across the country and reclaimed both chambers of Congress.

Carville, political adviser Mark McKinnon and Gen Z for Change founder Aidan Kohn-Murphy were talking about the potential for a post-President Trump GOP on Carville’s “ Politics War Room ” podcast when he made his claim about the Florida leader.

“The Republican winner last night was Ron DeSantis,” he said. “But Ron DeSantis can say we did better in — you know, ‘We want to win? Look at what we did in Florida’ … If I’m not a Republican, I don’t like Ron DeSantis … But everybody had dismissed him as out of hand.”

Carville noted that the Republican Party’s image will go down following Tuesday’s losses, but DeSantis’s “stock … doubled in the last 24 hours.” McKinnon chimed in, saying Florida’s and Texas’s results starkly differed, with Democrats making major gains in the Lone Star State while Republicans held firm in Florida, crediting DeSantis.

“The greatest beneficiary of this election may be Ron DeSantis,” he added.

Kohn-Murphy added that Democratic gains, but not wins, in Florida were “a pretty devastating result” that “could have been better.” But after seeing the Republican governor on the “national stage” before, the activist said he was unsure if “people will really take him seriously.”

DeSantis, who entered office in 2019 with Trump’s support and praise until the two faced off during the 2024 Republican presidential primary, has been seen as a potential successor to the president’s legacy. The Never Back Down PAC presented the governor as the future of the GOP in 2023.

Democrats gained ground in Florida state races and defeated Republican candidates for House seats, although the GOP maintained control of other major statewide offices. Voters chose Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) to succeed the term-limited DeSantis, becoming the Sunshine State’s first Black governor.

The outgoing Florida governor called the outcome of the midterms an “ extinction-level event ” for Republicans across the country while the party narrowly hung on to Florida.

“In January, when everyone in office leaves who are either term-limited or got voted out, of the 10 largest states in this union, only one state will have Republican control … the state of Florida,” he said at a press conference Wednesday.

DeSantis also diagnosed the election result as “no question … a rebuke of the president and the Congress by Democrats, independents and some Republicans that crossed over,” in an interview with Fox News’s Laura Ingraham later Wednesday.

“But a lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate,” he continued. “That’s just a fact. They were promised big things, and they didn’t deliver it.”

articles.title: Vance eyes 2028 reset, as Republicans mull pivot after US midterms drubbing
articles.summary: A Democratic ‘blue tsunami’ in the US midterms shines a light on emerging distaste for Trump’s brand among Republicans.
articles.body:
Hours after results confirmed that the Republican Party had lost control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in the United States Congress in the midterm elections this week, senior Republicans were hand-wringing over what had gone so badly wrong and whether a major course correction would now be required.

As once-Republican strongholds like Texas fell to the enemy, US Vice President JD Vance took to X to declare that the “real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone”.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance said.

Former Trump voters had switched sides, he said, over the Iran war and the US ties to Israel.

“I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, ‘I told you so’: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview,” he wrote.

Just days after the US and Israel launched strikes across Iran on February 28, Tehran effectively closed the critical Strait of Hormuz, which once transited roughly 25 percent of the world’s seaborne oil trade, triggering a massive spike in oil prices and a major global energy crisis. The price of Brent crude – the global benchmark – hit $120 in March and April and has hovered around $115 in recent weeks.

On Thursday morning, oil prices dropped to $93.82 a barrel on expectations that Republican Party losses would reduce the likelihood of US President Donald Trump renewing strikes on Iran following weeks of speculation.

But as consumers in the US struggle with sky-high petrol and diesel prices – not to mention the soaring cost of food, which has also been impacted by Trump’s trade tariffs – the midterms have forced a leadership rethink as the Trump brand appears increasingly toxic.

While no Republicans have declared their intention to run for the 2028 presidential election, some in the party are believed to be eyeing it now.

Andrew Payne, from the Chatham House think tank, told Al Jazeera that any Republican wanting to take on the 2028 election will now need to “distance themselves from the more unpopular aspects of Trump’s record”. That means the Iran war, the greatest poisoned chalice of them all.

“That, I think, is why Vance came out so clearly in blaming the war. It is evident to those who have been watching closely that he has always been the voice of scepticism behind the scenes, and he now needs to make that difference of opinion clear to the average voter. But doing so will be really hard while Trump is still in office and, presumably, wants to play an active role as kingmaker,” Payne said.

Unpopular, but not as unpopular as Trump

The most obvious pick and frontrunner for the Republican 2028 nomination is currently Vance, who is known to have ambitions to take over from Trump.

Regarded as an anti-US interventionist, Vance, while publicly supporting Trump’s Iran war, has also been privately urging him and others to end the conflict, according to the US news outlet Axios.

Last week, Vance sent a letter to the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei , proposing a meeting between US and Iranian officials soon in a bid to prevent further escalation. By contrast, this week Trump said the war would only come to an end “when I want it to”.

This move, coupled with his post on X on Wednesday night, is increasingly being seen as Vance putting as much distance as he can between himself and the war.

Throwing off the Trump touch may be trickier than he thinks, however, according to one Vance ally close to the White House who spoke to Politico on Wednesday. While it is “possible for him [Vance] to modestly differentiate himself” from Trump, the source said, there is no way to completely delink himself.

“He’s still Trump’s vice president. This is still a Trump administration war. They’re still both unpopular. He’s not as unpopular as Trump but he’s unpopular,” the anonymous source said.

According to Tuesday polling from The New York Times on who is ahead in a theoretical Republican presidential primary, Vance is at 40 percent. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio follows at 21 percent, alongside Donald Trump Jr, also at 21 percent.

Rubio has yet to comment on the Republican wipeout. Still, like Vance, he is allied with Trump’s administration, which may make a presidential bid challenging.

Any potential candidate now faces a choice between two routes, Payne said. One is to “re-energise the [Make America Great Again or MAGA] movement, which I expect will be difficult, because Trump did it through sheer force of personality that is hard to replicate”.

“The second route is to keep as much of the base on board as possible while appealing to the traditional conservative groups who have drifted from the party over the past decade, thereby expanding the coalition. If he runs, I would think Marco Rubio has a better shot at doing that,” Payne said.

There are other potential candidates to consider.

A former frontrunner for the 2016 presidential election, which saw Trump secure his first administration, Ted Cruz is now Texas’s only statewide Republican lawmaker.

In a post on X after the results, Cruz wrote: “2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. It was an a** kicking”.

“Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high. Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long. It should have been brief, decisive, and over,” Cruz wrote.

“Understandably, people were pissed off, and elected Republicans didn’t do enough to address their very real pain. So, what do we do now? We need to listen and respond. We need to champion economic policies that make a real difference in working people’s lives, and we need to deal with the consequences.”

In September, the Wall Street Journal reported that Cruz was testing the waters for the 2028 nomination. But as one of the early cheerleaders for the Iran war, Cruz will struggle to disassociate himself from it, other than to criticise the manner of its execution.

As the blame game continues, the Republican Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, described the results of the midterms as “close to an extinction-level event” for the party.

“If the Republican Party doesn’t have Texas as an anchor, then we are not going to be viable nationally going forward,” he said.

“We’re in a very volatile political era, things shift quickly, and the leaders just got to recognise that.”

DeSantis’s time as governor ends in January after two terms, but speculation has grown about whether he also wants to throw his hat into the ring for the US presidential nomination as the playing field remains wide open.

articles.title: Megyn Kelly: Time for GOP to learn how to win ‘without daddy’

articles.body:
Conservative pundit Megyn Kelly says the Republican Party has some soul-searching to do after this week’s midterm elections.

“This morning the Republican Party is in ruins, and maybe it needed to be,” Kelly said on her popular podcast and YouTube show.

“The choice now for Republicans is to reflect, rebuild, and reinvent in the image of no man. They’re going to have to do it on their own,” she continued. “They’re going to have to learn how to win without daddy on the ballot, and to find their ethical center, and not just be puppets of Trump’s, not to have their entire political world revolve around Donald Trump.”

The host’s comments were first highlighted by Mediaite .

Democrats won sweeping victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections, taking back control of the U.S. House and Senate and setting up major clashes with President Trump’s White House during his last two years in office.

Trump has sought to downplay GOP losses, insisting if he were on the ballot, the result would have been different, and he bemoaned a failure by Republicans to transfer their love for him to candidates for House and Senate.

Kelly has been sharply critical of Trump in recent months over the Iran war and its impact on the U.S. economy, a major factor in Tuesday’s midterm rout, which included Democratic Senate victories in long-held Republican strongholds including Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.

Potential GOP successors to Trump have also sought to blame the war for Tuesday’s results, including Vice President Vance and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who called the vote an “extinction-level event” for Republicans.

articles.title: 'Shock': Democrat flips deep-red House seat without airing a single TV ad as longtime Republican goes down
articles.summary: Victoria Broderick's upset of Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais mirrored Cyril Jefferson's North Carolina win as grassroots campaigns prevailed.
articles.body: Two years after losing to Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais by 43 points, Democrat Victoria Broderick flipped his deep-red Tennessee district by just 280 votes — despite spending under $100,000 and airing no paid TV ads. The victory ended DesJarlais’ 16-year congressional career. First elected in 2010, the Republican was seeking his ninth term in a district President Donald Trump carried by 24 points in 2024. The latest FEC figures available before Election Day show DesJarlais’ campaign spent $508,166 through Oct. 14, compared with just $90,062 for Broderick. His campaign also raised more than seven times as much as hers — $667,181 to $94,217 — yet the longtime incumbent still lost the deep-red seat. REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES Axios reported, citing AdImpact, that Broderick’s campaign had no record of airing paid television ads. Instead, she credited a grassroots operation that had been building for more than two years. Broderick was not the only Democrat to pull off a low-dollar House win. Axios also highlighted a similar upset in North Carolina, where High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson defeated Republican Rep. Addison McDowell 51.1% to 48.9%. Axios reported, citing AdImpact, that Jefferson had no tracked advertising spending, although a separate tracker lists $2,000 in Google ads, including YouTube placements. LEE CARTER: THE 5 WORDS THAT EXPLAIN THIS ELECTION BETTER THAN ANY COMMERCIAL McDowell had won the district by 38.3 points in 2024, according to election results. Broderick told Axios that her win was not a surprise to her team. "I know it was a shock for the rest of the country, but it wasn’t a shock for our team," she said. Jefferson similarly credited volunteers, saying, "You have to go engage them." Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), the sponsor of the original Epstein Files Transparency Act , said Thursday he felt confident he could force a vote on a follow-up bill once Congress returns following the election.

Massie wrote on the social platform X that he felt assured he would be able to get enough signatures for a discharge petition, which forces a vote on the House floor.

“When we return next week, we’ll get 218 signatures for Epstein Files Transparency Act II, which guarantees a vote,” he wrote.

“Survivors will be able to get their own records, State Attorneys General can prosecute crimes, and we can take the DOJ to court for keeping critical files hidden.”

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), the Democratic co-sponsor of the original legislation, called the new legislation the “Epstein 2.0 Act,” saying it would “allow state attorney generals to prosecute the pedophiles who abused and trafficked young girls.”

The Epstein Files Transparent Act received broad support in Congress and forced the Justice Department to release its millions of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

But survivors and other backers have called for greater transparency, including further redactions in the files as well as additional prosecutions of Epstein allies.

Massie and Khanna have asserted Epstein had additional co-conspirators who should face criminal charges.

articles.title: Trump has ‘transformed nothing that can’t be turned back the day after he leaves office’: Erick Erickson
articles.summary: Conservative radio host Erick Erickson warned that President Trump may have to work with Democrats in his final two years if he hopes to leave office with a stronger legislative record, calling his current agenda “impermanent.” “This is the most impermanent second term of any president in American history,” Erickson told NewsNation’s Leland Vittert. “Every…
articles.body:
Conservative radio host Erick Erickson warned that President Trump may have to work with Democrats in his final two years if he hopes to leave office with a stronger legislative record, calling his current agenda “impermanent.”

“This is the most impermanent second term of any president in American history,” Erickson told NewsNation’s Leland Vittert. “Every single thing the man has done other than a cryptocurrency bill , the Laken Riley Act and the tax bill have been by executive order. They can all be undone.”

Trump has broadly used executive orders to shape his second term agenda. He has avoided the use of Congress for some of his key policy initiatives like tariffs , regulating elections and birthright citizenship , most of which have been blocked by the Supreme Court.

The University of California Santa Barbara’s American Presidency Project tracks executive orders from presidents over time, and found that Trump in his second term is averaging 166 orders per year, a pace not seen since President Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Even when executive orders are not found unconstitutional, they can be easily undone by the next president. One example is the Paris climate agreement, which Trump pulled out of in his first term, which former President Biden reversed on his first day in office. Trump then left again during the first week of his second term.

Erickson said Republicans should worry that the president may work with Democrats on legislation that is more permanent so that history looks favorably upon him.

“[The orders] can all be undone unless he does cut some deals with the Democrats,” Erickson told the “On Balance” host. “He wants credit in history for being a transformational president. He’s transformed nothing that can’t be turned back the day after he leaves office.”

Trump told the Wall Street Journal on election night that he was willing to work with Democrats but acknowledged his ability to veto anything they pass.

The president will have to work with Democrats to get anything passed out of Congress after the party’s landslide election victory . Democrats will begin the 120th Congress with at least 54 Senate seats and 251 House seats, according to Decision Desk HQ’s projections, and they lead in more races that have yet to be called.

Still, the “Erick Erickson Show” host was skeptical that Democrats would make an effort to work with Trump.

“I don’t know that the Democrats are willing to work with him. I think they want to spend their time investigating,” Erickson said. “The Democrats believe they’ve been affirmed back into their righteousness as well.”

“The only thing that I can guarantee about this election is neither side is going to win or understand the right lessons,” he added. “And that’s going to drive further rage of the voters.”

articles.title: Pritzker says it seems like ‘number one cheerleader’ Vance is breaking from Trump
articles.summary: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D), who won his third term as the governor of the Prairie State, criticized Vice President Vance’s social media post following the Republican party’s sweeping losses in the midterm elections saying Vance cannot “run away from what he’s been.” “Well, let’s face it, JD Vance has been Donald Trump’s number one…
articles.body:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D), who won his third term as the governor of the Prairie State, criticized Vice President Vance’s social media post following the Republican party’s sweeping losses in the midterm elections saying Vance cannot “run away from what he’s been.”

“Well, let’s face it, JD Vance has been Donald Trump’s number one cheerleader,” Pritzker said during an appearance on CNN. “He’s supported everything about the president. Now he wants to seem like he’s breaking with the president.”

Vance on Wednesday , in a lengthy social media post , put the blame of the Republican party’s midterm losses on the ongoing war in Iran. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” he said.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he argued.

The post came after Democrats took control of both the House and the Senate for the next term in the midterm elections, securing major wins in battleground states like Texas, Michigan, Ohio, Maine, Kansas and Iowa.

During his CNN appearance, Pritzker also noted that Vance was “sticking up for Vivek Ramaswamy’s terrible ad attacking a woman who had been raped when she was 12 years old,” referring to an attack ad launched by the Republican gubernatorial nominee’s campaign against the winning Democrat Amy Acton ahead of the elections.

The ad featured Acton’s estranged mother, who called her daughter a “liar” and urged Ohioans to vote against her. Acton has previously opened up about experiencing physical and sexual abuse during her childhood. Her mother stayed with her stepfather after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton when she was 12 years old.

It received widespread criticism across the board, but Vance slammed the critics and stood behind Ramaswamy saying he “had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar.”

“I think he’s got a lot to answer for. I don’t think he can run away from what he’s been,” Pritzker said during his CNN appearance.

Massie told CNN earlier that he plans to call for a vote to…
articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has sparred with his own party in the past year, said Thursday morning that his call to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is “a much gentler version” of what can happen when Democrats take control of Congress.

Massie told CNN earlier that he plans to call for a vote to impeach Hegseth. In a post on social platform X on Wednesday night, Massie said, “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns.”

On Thursday morning, Massie posted on social platform X saying “my Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress. They’ll have hearings & trials.”

The discussion surrounding Hegseth comes after the Democrats took control of the House and the Senate in a sweeping victory in the midterm elections where they secured historic wins in battleground states like Texas, Iowa, Ohio, Michigan and Maine, among others.

CBS News on Wednesday reported that President Trump has been asking advisers and allies whether Hegseth should stay in his role following the midterms. The president said Wednesday that he is not considering replacing the Defense Secretary adding, “he’s doing a very good job.”

The Hill previously reported that Hegseth is interested in the open Tennessee Senate seat and has been campaigning behind the scenes for the post. When asked if he would want Hegseth to fill Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s (R-Tenn.) seat, Trump said that he would “be very popular if he did that. But I haven’t heard that at all.”

Massie, in his Thursday morning post, said if the president is “going to replace appointees like Hegseth, he should do it while he can still get the replacements confirmed in the Senate.”

Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) speaks with reporters outside the House Chamber after discussing his privileged resolution of eight impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Sept. 16, 2026. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) announced the House would leave a day earlier than expected which would prevent his motion from being voted on.
